items.body: In musical notation, al niente means “to nothing”: a gradual fading until sound disappears. The title suits this debut by Beatrice Miniaci, Cosimo Fiaschi, Gabriele Pagliano and Luca Venitucci, a quartet whose music is shaped by subtraction. Three collective improvisations sit alongside compositions by Stefan Thut and Pagliano, with gestures pared down to small fluctuations of breath, timbre and silence. The four musicians rarely behave as separate voices. In the accompanying interview, they describe coming to think of the ensemble as “one instrument instead of the sum of four different voices”, an approach that can be heard throughout the record. Flute, soprano saxophone, accordion and double bass converge into shifting composite timbres, occasionally separating long enough for an individual instrumental character to surface before being absorbed again. Stefan Thut’s “Some, 1–4” uses an extremely limited vocabulary of sound and noise to produce a surprisingly fluid landscape. Small differences in duration and articulation create movement within a score that otherwise appears almost static. Pagliano’s “Umbra” is similarly economical, tracing the relationship between a gesture and its “shadow” through minute changes in resonance. Extended techniques belong to the music’s basic vocabulary: pitch gives way to breath, friction and resonance, while instrumental identities become increasingly uncertain. Silence has an active role throughout. Venitucci describes it as a continuous field from which individual sounds acquire their presence, and the album makes that relationship unusually tangible. An attack or breath changes the space around it; a resonance continues to register as it approaches inaudibility. In the closing minutes of the final improvisation, the double bass briefly emerges on its own before the other instruments return and the music slowly thins away, approaching the niente of the title. AL NIENTE – photo by Alessandro Carpentieri To guide us towards silence, we reached out directly to Cosimo Fiaschi, Beatrice Miniaci, Gabriele Pagliano, and Luca Venitucci. Listening to al niente, I often lost track of where one instrument ended and another began. The quartet continually reshapes itself into a single, evolving timbre before individual voices briefly re-emerge. Even in the collective improvisations, there’s very little sense of anyone stepping forward as a soloist. Is that something you consciously cultivate, or does it simply emerge from the way each of you listens and responds to the others? The ensamble: Reducing the material down to its bare bones often implies unison, where one instrument is the continuation of the other. In a way, it felt natural to investigate the unison of four very different instruments, that do not share any (?) musical literature. Probably the idea of soloist ceased to be valid while working primarily with long tones and silences. In both improvisations and repertoire, it seems way more interesting to think of the quartet as one instrument instead of the sum of four different voices. The music we made deals with few musical parameters in which details plays a crucial role: but a sharp attack or a little crescendo, for example, could also be the sings of a more prominent musical action which could be understand as some sort of soloist role. In the last track of the album, at approximately six minutes the double-bass introduces the final with a brief solo. That action, for instance, could be understood as a soloist role, since it’s the only one with articulation, in the sense of density. Stefan Thut describes “Some, 1–4” as a score in which the notated image seems to liquefy when it is brought into sound, only to return repeatedly to its original static form. Listening to the piece, I had the impression that the music was constantly oscillating between movement and stillness, almost as if the score itself were breathing. As performers, how did you approach that balance? Did the notation leave room for individual interpretation, or did it require a very precise collective discipline? The ensamble: First of all, we really have to thank Stefan Thut for his availability and for agreeing to share his work with us. The piece consists of four combinations of the letters x and y, where x is sound and y is noise. We choose this piece for its simplicity within the relation sound / noise, as well as the interest in contingencies, since the individual sound and noise (one for every musician in both categories) are chosen a priori. The piece needs an individual discipline since each performer chooses only one of the four permutation (that is also chosen a priori): sound / sound; sound / noise; noise / sound; noise / noise. The oscillation between movement ad stillness you were referring to is generated through the different durations that each of us gave to each sound / noise. In this sense, it’s amazing how a very limited material (six different musical objects within four performers) can create such movements. Both the flute and the soprano saxophone seem to occupy a particularly unstable position on the album. At various moments they cease to function as melodic instruments and instead become sources of breath, friction, multiphonics and noise, often blurring the distinction between pitched sound and pure timbre. How has your relationship with your instruments changed through working with al niente? Has this ensemble altered the way you think about tone production itself? Beatrice Miniaci and Cosimo Fiaschi: The constellation of al niente (four acoustic instruments without resonances) is the perfect setting to let the subtle characteristics of the flute, bass flute and soprano saxophone emerge through the techniques you mentioned. The air quality is a particular trait d’union between the overall ensemble: the accordion is an aerophone too and the double-bass with the archetto is capable of producing many air sounds. Generally speaking, the overall dryness of the quartet in the discreet dynamics is the ideal setting to dig into the liminal zone between air and pitch for our instruments. Pagliano, in your notes on “Umbra”, you describe the relationship between a sound and its “shadow”, referring to positive and negative sounds almost as if they were photographic images. Listening to the piece, I was struck by the fact that these shadows never feel electronic or artificial; they seem to emerge naturally from the instruments themselves. When composing “Umbra”, were you thinking primarily in terms of acoustics and resonance, or was the idea of the “shadow” also a way of exploring the relationship between action, memory and listening? Gabriele Pagliano: Thank you for you deep listening. The core of this piece can be find in the gesture, or action, as a musical object. Every possible reflection about resonance or acoustic spectrum originates from there: the possibilities that come from the process of transformation, or permutation of a single or composed gesture. Even if the sonic texture has to take a central role in the performer thinking, the compositional approach revolves around this idea more than a spectralist approach in a narrow sense. In this perspective, the fact that we never feel these shadow parts “artificial” it’s a welcomed consequence; I think that the realm of the acoustic instruments it’s were the borders between sound and silence are the closest possible and in this sense the gesture is the device that naturally activates that relationship. Venitucci, with more than three decades of experience in experimental music, you’ve worked in contexts ranging from free improvisation to contemporary composition. What fascinates me about al niente is its refusal to treat quietness as simply the absence of sound. Silence often feels active, almost as if it were another performer shaping the music. Has your understanding of silence changed over the years, and what does this ensemble allow you to explore that other improvising groups perhaps do not? Luca Venitucci: My early approach to sound was shaped by rock and European improvised music of the 1960s and 1970s, and naturally tended towards rather assertive gestures. Later, through Ensemble Zeitkratzer, I came into contact with the Wandelweiser movement and Berlin’s Echtzeitmusik scene, which led me to develop a deeper awareness of silence, not as a mere absence of sound, but as a continuous field from which each sonic event emerges and takes on depth and presence. In al niente, this focus on silence brings the finest qualities of sound into the foreground, revealing the subtle transformations and inflections that arise from each musician’s intentions and from their interaction. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. A distinctly futuristic sense of movement Revealed several months ago in April 2026, this sleek eight-piece suite (titled Disruptive Event) still carries a sense of propulsion and precise direction. From its opening moments, Signal_Black (aka Marcin) establishes a dense exchange between analog glitch and Autechre-influenced sound-design, immediately evident on “Higher Ground.” From there, the project descends deep below terra firma, evolving through scraped emotive melodic fragments and moving further into ambient-industrial IDM abstraction. A fixation on roughened rhythms and microscopic melodic fibers gives “Internal Merge” its distinctive tension, folding broken structures into looping forms that gradually become cohesive without losing their instability. “Long Now” shifts toward wobbling bass pressure, while “TON” sinks into darker ambient territory, and what becomes more evident is that each track extends the artist’s interest in malfunction, texture, and controlled disorientation. As the final pieces move through old-school Arovane-like finesse, especially on “Text of The Present,” “Chronic” delivers a more microscopic form of sonic deformation. Its fractured detail reflects the album’s central idea: a disruptive event capable of interrupting established operations, routines, or systems. Rather than treating glitch as surface decoration, Signal_Black builds an entire skeletal language around it. What emerges is a unified, tightly constructed collection of focused (yet splintered) electronics—one that pushes exploratory sound forward through distortion, fragmentation, and a distinctly futuristic sense of movement. While Disruptive Event channels our favored old-school IDM mechanics associated with Richard Devine, Gescom, Funckarma, Alva Noto, SND, and Funkstörung, Signal_Black takes that lineage somewhere altogether stranger—refining tone, deepening texture, and redirecting momentum into a galaxy of its own. items.body: That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. A duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone [PCLLP 037] Axial Opposition by Multiplex   Multiplex are brothers Christian and Roland Dormon, their focused frenzy of pulsating electronics sees no barriers, but always anchored by a deep melodic instinct. Emerging from IDM’s early days more than two decades ago—recall their releases with Toytronic, Senton, Piehead, and U-Cover)— they now find a home with Belarus-based People Can Listen following recent releases Colour Kinetica (Bricolage) and Human, I Love You (w/ Remixes) (Clean Error). Their historical relevance remains an important factoid for anyone new to sandblasted, ever-veering strains of broken beats, IDM, and melodic electro, yet beneath those fractured forms is where Multiplex have always been most distinctive: tuneful synthesis, layered with ambient propulsion and shaped into electronic structures that feel both precise and uniquely alive. Axial Opposition opens with punishing electro, eerily transcendental in its summation of the 42-second opener “Reality (Interlude),” before settling into their bread-and-butter language of pristine melodies, glowing synth lines, and carefully interlocked sound design textures. Synthesizers are not simply used as rhythmic machinery here; they carry the emotional weight, allowing melodies to drift, repeat, fracture, and return with a nostalgic clarity. That sensibility comes to life across favorites such as “In Your Dreams,” “Pulsar Energy,” “Verhn,” “Aditya,” and “Neeta_x,” before dissolving into the closing atmospheric layers of “Implode (outro).” “What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character.” ~Pietro Da Sacco With 24 years now behind Pinghaus Frequencies (Toytronic), alongside earlier productions dating to 1999, Multiplex have long signalled a duo creating electronics with melody as its backbone. Axial Opposition gathers new and vintage material after more than 15 years of silence, sending music back and forth between studios, adding elements along the way and shaping everything into a final mix. What makes the collection compelling is how naturally those eras communicate: older synth ideas are not merely revived, but repolished, expanded, and brought into the present without losing their original character. That exchange between past and present is central to Axial Opposition. Classic Multiplex structures remain recognizable, yet the melodic synthesis gives them renewed dimension, allowing vintage electronic language to exist alongside contemporary detail. There is nostalgia here, but it never feels archival; sounds that might have belonged to another era are given fresh circuitry, fresh atmosphere, and a new context. After such a long silence, Multiplex return not by abandoning what made their sound distinctive, but by reconnecting with it and pushing it forward. A multiverse of melodic electronics, where old synthesis is made new again, and one that only Multiplex can navigate so well. Axial Opposition is available on People Can Listen. items.body: What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. Moments of tenderness appear inside the delicate violence Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back   South Korea’s Wona returns in a different spacesuit with Headphone Beats 2025-2026 by Winter Back, an album that feels less like a collection of tracks than a future archetype: a visceral, crystal-clear demonstration of what electronic sound work can become when technique, instinct and design aesthetics are allowed to mutate together. I’d hazard a guess it was made through a pair of headphones over the course of a year, because there’s something intensely close-up about it—and the title proposed, eh? On the surface, you might identify glitch aesthetics, but that’s only the doorway. Beneath it are drill and trap rhythms, tensile funk, lo-fi breakbeat trippery, obfuscation, drops, crescendos, proto-brass, rolling bass and complex and simple synthesis that seems perpetually on the verge of becoming something else. I’m genuinely thrilled this landed on my figurative desk. It’s remorselessly stunning. “Matmat” has my heart: thunderous, rolling beats tumble around each other in waterfalls of hugeness and electrification while the low end holds you prisoner. “AGN” stinks—in the very best sense. Its half-time stutter is a screwface anthem of dropping beat and bass pulse, scratch-and-tear music so filthy you can almost smell it. Backward melodies emerge from the darkness to lighten the load, moments of tenderness appearing inside the delicate violence. “There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved.” ~Will Wonks And this is the crucial distinction: this isn’t impenetrable sound design made to impress other sound designers. It’s a highly informed, deeply nuanced deviance in sound, rhythm and strata. Our title track “Winter Back” demonstrates an enviable approach to drum programming before its apparent mid-point collapse detonates into a spanking groove of epic proportions—the holy grail of contemporary electronic funk. “TLD” may contain the most outrageous break on the record, somehow folding rhythm back into itself and emerging as something entirely new: a funky drummer for 3026. Nearly every track appears to reach a point where it dissolves, sheds its skin and reconstitutes somewhere else. These aren’t conventional breakdowns so much as dimensional ruptures. “Bedrop” is the perfect example: atmosphere and tense pads briefly suspend the album in mid-air before the future-klaxon begins its nagging ascent and the whole thing lurches forward again. “Set Jen” brings tribal toms and deranged circus bells into some kind of beautifully unstable agreement. “Dedication” removes the floor entirely, a beatless blast of aural oxygen that makes the subsequent savagery hit harder. “Starb” and “Still Ago” sound like saucepans being thrown down the stairs through a malfunctioning computer, grinding the listener into submission, before “220” closes the circuit with single hi-hits, elastic wubs and a sense of space suddenly expanding beyond the edges of the record. What makes Headphone Beats 2025-2026 so exciting is that it never settles into its own language. Every time you think you’ve identified the rules, it quietly moves the goalposts. Genres are treated less as destinations than as raw materials: broken apart, stretched, folded, obscured and rebuilt into strange new functional objects. There is beauty in the abrasion and an almost ridiculous confidence in allowing sounds to seem to remain unresolved. It feels experimental without announcing itself as experimental. It feels futuristic without resorting to the usual sci-fi vocabulary. Most importantly, it feels alive. It’s a great example of electronic music one would want to spend time inside, not simply consume. The deeper you go, the more its internal architecture reveals itself: tiny rhythmic decisions, concealed transitions, unexpected pockets of funk, bass frequencies that seem to have their own gravitational field. It rewards repeated listening because it keeps changing shape under examination. You don’t exhaust it; you develop a better understanding of how much is actually happening. A genuinely extraordinary piece of work. A 10/10 proposition where nothing is missing and nothing needs adding. Rare. Welcomed. Headphone Beats 2025-2026 is available on SoundSupply_Service. items.body: Amamere come from Cape Coast, the Fante fishing port where Ebo Taylor and C.K. Mann were born, and they play highlife the way Ghana’s guitar bands played it in the 1970s. Eric Asiedu Agyekum‘s lead guitar sits out front, tenor sax and trumpet play over the top, and behind the kit is Rim Akandoh Jnr, who spent the late 2010s drumming for Taylor. Their live take on “Kokonsani”, the opening track of the 2025 debut Man Shall Be Free on Afro Urban Project, was filmed at Afrika Festival Hertme in the Netherlands on 4 July, during the eight-piece’s first tour outside Ghana. Dominic Ansah plays Ga kpanlogo drums and congas under the kit, and the trumpet belongs to Emmanuel Adjei, grandson of Osibisa‘s Mac Tontoh. Akandoh Jnr’s father, Rim Akandoh, played in Mann’s band before leading the Prince Sparrows Band. Much of the album reworks his songs alongside osode, the fishing-community music Mann electrified, while “Kokonsani”, Twi for a gossip, carries the son’s own lyric. items.body: Düsseldorf and Electronic music have been inextricably linked for decades. The city has produced a distinctive musical legacy in which experimentation, electronics, minimalism, and a fascination with the future have always been central. It is a history that stretches back to the 1970s and 1980s, when electronic music, with Kraftwerk as its pioneering flagship, was not so much regarded as an exercise in nostalgia, but rather as a way of looking towards the future. It was within this tradition that Mängelexemplar emerged in 2011, simply abbreviated as MNGLXMPLR. The Düsseldorf duo, consisting of Lilli B. and Joa H., found their place in the international underground with a distinctive blend of Minimal-Wave and Electro-Pop. Their name — stripped of its vowels to become the almost cryptic MNGLXMPLR — seems perfectly suited to their musical universe: sleek, unconventional, and just a little elusive. Over the years, MNGLXMPLR have established themselves as a familiar name on the scene, performing at numerous festivals and venues both in Germany and abroad. With their new album, “Neue Zukunft,” released this spring on Infacted Recordings, they continue their exploration of Minimal-Wave, delivering an opus that feels darker, harder, and more intense. I spoke with both protagonists about the album, their musical journey, and the future of MNGLXMPLR. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Q: MNGLXMPLR has now been active for more than ten years. Looking back, what are the first thoughts that come to mind? What have been the defining moments or biggest highlights so far, and how would you say the band has evolved over the years? M:More than ten years… that’s quite a statement. The funny thing is, there was never a ten-year plan. We founded MNGLXMPLR because we wanted to make music. One year became five, five became ten – and suddenly here we are. There have been intense phases, quiet phases, great shows, frustrating moments, and countless ideas that never made it anywhere. That’s part of it. The biggest change is probably that we’ve become much more confident in our own musical language. In the beginning, there was more searching and experimenting. Today, we have a much better sense of what feels right for MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to turn that into a formula. The moment you know exactly what the next track is going to sound like, things become boring. There have been many highlights over the years – releases, concerts, travels and encounters that happened through the music. But the biggest highlight is actually very simple: we’re still here. And we’re still curious. Q: It took several years for “Neue Zukunft” to finally see the light of day. I imagine that period brought about changes – not only in terms of your studio setup, but also in your songwriting and creative process. Could you tell us a little about how you have evolved and how that development shaped the album? M:“Neue Zukunft” took its time. A lot changed at Carismastudios during those years. The studio evolved, new equipment was added, different projects emerged, and we experimented with different ways of working. Some of those experiments eventually became part of the album. There are tracks that existed for years before they found their final form. We kept coming back to them, changing things, removing things, and sometimes simply leaving them alone for a while. Our songwriting has become more intuitive over time. We don’t sit down and say, ‘Today we’re going to write a minimal track’. A song can start with a beat, a sound, a voice, or simply a certain mood. The emotional side has also become more important. We wanted the emotion to already be present in the music, rather than being added later through production. The result has become harder and more direct in some places, but the minimalist foundation has remained. And we have no problem with a few rough edges. For us, perfect doesn’t automatically mean interesting. Q: What can you tell us about “Neue Zukunft”? What is the central idea or concept behind the album, and how do you look back on the composition, recording and production process today? M:“Neue Zukunft” is about change and movement. It’s not a concept album in the classic sense. There isn’t one single story that you have to decode. It’s more like a collection of different moods and sides of MNGLXMPLR. Minimalist structures, darker atmospheres, harder sounds and emotional moments. We wanted to preserve these contrasts. The visual identity also became an important part of the album. For this, we are working with Düsseldorf fashion icon Ela Holscher, fashion designer Michaela Reinhardt-Beron and photographer Thomas Stelzmann. In Düsseldorf, music, fashion, photography and art have always been closely connected. So for us, this connection felt very natural. But we didn’t want to turn it into nostalgia. We have no interest in pretending it’s 1982 again. Düsseldorf has its history. We’re interested in what we can do with it today. This idea is also carried onto the stage. Sound, visuals, fashion and performance should become part of the same atmosphere. Q: The title “Neue Zukunft” immediately catches the eye – particularly at a time shaped by increasing geopolitical tensions, social uncertainty and war. At the same time, we are entering a new artistic era in which algorithms, AI and digital technologies are increasingly influencing how music is created and consumed. What does the title “Neue Zukunft” mean to you, and how does it reflect your view of the world today? M:We deliberately wanted a title that looks ahead. There is already enough dystopian language around us. Of course, we see what is happening in the world. War, political conflicts and uncertainty are part of the present. But “Neue Zukunft” is not about resignation. It’s about movement. The future is coming anyway. AI is obviously part of that future and is already changing the way music is created and consumed. We don’t use AI to create MNGLXMPLR. For us, the human process remains essential: writing, playing, recording, making mistakes and changing things. Electronic music, however, has always been closely connected to technological change. Synthesizers, samplers and computers changed the way musicians work. AI will be another major shift. We don’t think it makes sense to simply accept it blindly or reject it outright. You have to question it. You have to decide what you want to use from it and why. “Neue Zukunft” doesn’t mean that we know what tomorrow will look like. It means that we’re ready to find out. Q: These days, many listeners focus more on playlists and individual singles than on complete albums. I personally still believe that an album represents a comprehensive artistic statement. Do you think the album format remains relevant in an increasingly fragmented and fast-paced musical landscape? M:Absolutely. A single can work on its own. But an album gives it context. You can build an atmosphere, create tension and connect tracks that might work very differently as individual singles. That’s important to us. “Neue Zukunft” was made as an album, and the sequence of the tracks matters. And then there’s the album on vinyl. We like the physical experience. You take the record out of the sleeve, look at the artwork, put it on and listen. Then you turn it over. You can’t really speed that up. And maybe that’s exactly the point. In a world where everything is instantly available, a record forces you to slow down. You can even hold the music in your hands. Artwork, photography, design and music become one shared object. That still has value. Q: MNGLXMPLR is also very much a live band – you have even played in Belgium three times already. How important are live performances to your identity as a band? How do you transfer the atmosphere of your studio recordings to the stage, and what touring plans do you have in connection with “Neue Zukunft”? M:Playing live is extremely important to us. The studio is controlled; the stage isn’t. That’s exactly why we like it. We don’t want to simply reproduce “Neue Zukunft” live exactly as it sounds on the record. The live versions are more direct, more physical and sometimes even harder. But the atmosphere has to remain intact. The audience also changes the performance. You can prepare a set, but you can’t prepare a room. We’ve already played in Belgium three times, and every concert had its own character. That’s one of the reasons we enjoy playing abroad. With “Neue Zukunft”, we want to play a new series of concerts across Europe. Looking towards 2027, we also want to move beyond the classic minimal scene, discover other Electronic scenes and play larger stages. The visual side will also become more important. Not as decoration, but as part of the performance. Sound, light, fashion, photography and movement should belong together. We don’t want people to simply hear “Neue Zukunft”. We want them to experience it. Q: You come from Düsseldorf, a city that will forever be associated with KRAFTWERK. To what extent do you still feel this artistic legacy among Electronic artists from the city today? Has Düsseldorf’s musical heritage directly or indirectly influenced your own work? M:Kraftwerk is unavoidable. If you make Electronic music in Düsseldorf, you grow up with that history. But Düsseldorf is much more than Kraftwerk. DAF, Die Krupps and many other artists developed completely different forms of electronic music. What connects them for us isn’t necessarily a particular sound. It’s an attitude: experimenting, reducing, making music physical, questioning things, and not caring too much whether someone has already invented a genre for it. We can relate to that a lot. But we don’t want to sound like Kraftwerk, or DAF, or Die Krupps. They’ve already done that – and pretty well. So our connection to Düsseldorf’s musical history is more indirect. You grow up surrounded by music, art, fashion, photography and clubs. You absorb that environment without necessarily realizing it. And years later, you realize how much of it has stayed with you. So yes, Düsseldorf has influenced MNGLXMPLR. But we don’t want to become a heritage band. We respect the past, but musically, we live in the here and now. Look back. Take with you what matters. Keep moving forward.

items.body: Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo that, following a debut album released on Electric Underground Records, is now self-releasing its second opus. I don’t recall ever hearing anything by them before, but these 13 tracks provide a clear picture of the duo’s musical identity. Their primary influences clearly lie within the realm of old-school EBM—specifically the kind of EBM characterized by thoughtful composition and well-crafted arrangements. The vocals, and indeed some of the tracks, remind me somewhat of Portion Control, while other songs reveal traces of Skinny Puppy’s influence. One track even feels like a nod to Front 242. It should be noted that these are all bands with highly distinctive sounds and complex structures. Kommission Z80 doesn’t quite reach that level yet; they would benefit from improving some technical aspects, particularly the mixing and recording. Nevertheless, there is undeniable potential here. Several strong tracks are waiting to be discovered, and the latter part of the album, in particular, features some very cool songs. Kommission Z80 is a name that true EBM enthusiasts should remember. (Rating:7). Listen to “Here Comes The Consequences”: Here Comes The Consequences by Kommission Z80 About Kommission Z80 Kommission Z80 is a Swedish duo from Borås formed by Erik Holmberg and Fredrich Legnemark, working in an old-school EBM style. The project’s debut single “Empire” arrived in 2024 through Electric Underground Records, followed by the debut album “Hegemony” and the “Reasonable Conclusions” EP in 2025. “Sic Semper Tyrannis” is the duo’s self-released 2026 follow-up.

items.body: I went to bed I saw you there You shook your head It’s all out, where? There is a special cruelty in being wounded by someone who has already left the room. The accusation lands, the door closes, and suddenly one person possesses the luxury of departure while the other inherits everything that remains unresolved. They replay every sentence, defend themselves to an empty room, and search for the words they were never allowed to speak. Kind Kid’s latest single bleed inhabits precisely that imbalance, turning abandonment into a bright, brisk synthpop song whose surface seems almost indecently cheerful beside the injury underneath. The arrangement draws its movement from eighties synthpop and its darker hues from the gothic electronics of Clan of Xymox to the Modern Darkwave sensibilities of Boy Harsher, with eerie synth flourishes and cold, uneasy tones curling around a dark disco beat. The rhythm keeps the song moving toward the dance floor, though something in those keyboards suggests the argument will be waiting when you get home. Julien Martinez sings from the position of someone denied the final word, his sense of injury finding an accomplice in the music’s disquiet. That tension gives “bleed” its emotional force: the hooks offer release while the synths keep returning to the bruise. The lyrics are deliberately circular. Images return, phrases repeat, and the speaker seems trapped inside an encounter that has ended everywhere except in his own mind. Repetition becomes psychological rather than decorative, suggesting those arguments one continues hours later while washing dishes, driving home, or staring at the ceiling, inventing increasingly perfect replies for someone who is no longer listening. “I thought of it as some metaphorical situation where someone’s been left behind after some sort of attack… left to “bleed,” muses Kind Kid frontman Julien Martinez. “Sometimes a situation can feel so much different to one person than the other.” One person may regard an argument as a momentary discharge of anger; the other can experience the same exchange as an injury requiring days to understand. bleed catches that disparity without weighing down its pop architecture. Its hooks remain airy, almost playful, while the words circle rejection, exposure, and helplessness. items.body: Are we better off alone Will I come into my own Are we better off alone Being understood by someone is a comfort until the relationship ends and their imagined opinion starts conducting an inspection of everything wrong with you. Boy Harsher’s Faulty inhabits that uncomfortable interval between asking to be wanted and wondering what that wanting has cost. Jae Matthews sings as though the verdict may already be in, while Augustus Muller gives her doubts enough room to move. The question of being better off alone becomes something to turn over on the dancefloor, where thinking clearly has always been optional. The song accompanies the release of Get Mean, out now following its September 18 arrival through Atlantic Records. Their first album since 2022’s The Runner, the twelve-track record follows the end of Matthews and Muller’s romantic relationship in early 2024, after a period of family loss, personal upheaval, and creative uncertainty. Continuing the band meant finding a way to work together while the terms of their lives were changing. That makes the tenderness of Faulty particularly affecting: the people making this music understand how complicated its questions can become. A kicking beat, busy hi-hats, and quivering synths set Faulty in motion. Its dark disco rhythm has some of Careful’s physical insistence, softened by broad synth pads and little descending electronic notes that drop through the arrangement with a rounded, almost playful boop. When the beat pauses to breathe, the synths take on a Vangelis-like warble, briefly opening the song into something more spacious and cinematic. The rhythm returns beneath a lead synth that bends up and down in pitch, while Matthews keeps her voice hushed and close, breathing the words with a tenderness that borders on resignation. The lyrics put affection and self-assessment in an uncomfortable room together. Asking whether she is faulty gives another person the power to diagnose her; asking whether she will come into her own begins to take some of that power back. Repetition keeps either possibility from becoming a settled conclusion. Matthews sounds caught between wanting to be held and recognizing how much of herself might be waiting outside the relationship. Directed by Boy Harsher and shot on 35mm with cinematography by Owen Smith-Clark, the final video in the Get Mean series returns to a room lined in brown wood paneling. A television glows blue on a black stand, a small fan sits by the window, and a microphone cable trails across the carpet. Against that ordinary setting, the changing cast look dressed for entirely different evenings: a white cowboy hat, metallic bodysuits, striped knitwear, black boots. Each person seems to have brought a private version of the same bad night. The camera moves from fixed views of the room into close-ups of faces, hands, and bodies moving past one another. People share the frame, lean together, or briefly touch, but proximity never quite settles the question in the chorus. There is a lovely awkwardness to it: the self-consciousness of dancing at home, followed by the sudden absorption of forgetting you are being watched. By the end, the people have gone and the television is still there. The room has held all that feeling without offering anyone an answer. Watch the video for Faulty below: Across Get Mean, the effort to keep going takes several musical forms. Writing began to move again when Matthews took to the road, travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, and South Florida. The album was eventually recorded in eight locations across the United States, Mexico, and Italy, its unsettled circumstances allowing new sounds and approaches into the duo’s work. Matthews describes it as “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The three singles we covered ahead of its release made clear how much that offering could contain. The first indication came with Jeans, released in June. Its springy guitar figure and bubbling electronics brought a new wave directness to Boy Harsher, with a steel-slide twang giving the song a western accent. Our earlier comparison to the Pretenders still fits the way Matthews’ cool delivery rides that guitar, while the buoyancy also suggests Muller’s work in Safe Mind. Beneath the cheek is a sharp little study of ambition: the dream of escaping a small town, the dream of becoming somebody, and the possibility of ending up selling an image of freedom by the pair. The band’s latex line-dancing video, conceived with Robert Palmer’s Addicted to Love in mind, makes that collision between aspiration, performance, and merchandise deliciously literal. Hard Beat, unveiled alongside July’s album announcement, tightens the pressure around a repeating bass-synth figure and an unrelenting kick. As we noted then, there is something of Depeche Mode’s Behind the Wheel in its meeting of motion, desire, and surrendered control. Matthews moves between confession and invitation while the rhythm keeps pushing ahead. Its video makes those exchanges physical through an elaborate leg brace, a Cadillac, and a handheld camcorder, drawing medical hardware, automotive controls, and the invasive act of filming into the same uneasy visual language. Within the album, the track preserves the severe club momentum that has long served Boy Harsher so well, giving the softer and more openly melodic songs something solid to push against. August’s Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) puts a warmer arrangement around the indignity of waiting for someone to remember you exist. A brisk new wave beat, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and short bursts of distorted guitar carry Matthews’ unhappy drawl toward the sort of pop chorus that can make despair briefly feel sociable. Her insistence that she is okay sounds increasingly like something she needs to practice. Our earlier review followed that idea into the lyric video, where yellow karaoke lettering crosses the blue screen of a CRT television. Created with vintage video equipment by Sean McGuirk and shot by Jesse Korman, it turns failed communication into a singalong with nobody else visibly present. Heard beside Faulty, the song makes the eventual question of solitude feel earned. Coming Home opens with Matthews in a smoky, Lynchian register, her voice suspended over steadily repeating synths and a breezy dance beat. The low guitar tones bring New Order to mind, with the melodic weight of a Peter Hook bassline translated onto guitar. That combination gives the song an appealing pull between bodily ease and emotional uncertainty. The rhythm leaves the windows open; the vocal suggests someone still deciding whether it is safe to come inside. Here, the album’s broader musical interests allow vulnerability to sound inviting without making it seem simple. Ice Pick (Walk Away) makes a particularly satisfying turn toward gothic rock. The parenthetical invites a Sisters of Mercy comparison before the guitar has even had its say, and the melody strengthens the association with their First and Last and Always period. A deep post-punk bass groove and the crunchy splash of the drum machine give the track a familiar dry ice chill. Matthews’ tender delivery moderates that severity, placing a vulnerable voice inside an arrangement with its collar firmly turned up. The resemblance is a pleasure to hear, especially from a duo whose love of this music has often been expressed through a different set of instruments. Pray 4 Me lets the bass loosen its hips. Soft synth pads, a sexy funk groove, and quivering bell tones bring a strain of Bryan Ferry-eque sophisti-pop into the album, expanding its capacity for pleasure as well as distress. There is a suppleness to the arrangement that makes this feel like a natural extension of the record’s emotional dynamic range. Desire, after all, does not become less complicated when somebody gives it a particularly good bassline. Boy Harsher sounds comfortable letting elegance and appetite share the same song. The album closes with Bleed, setting trip-hop beats against crystalline synths and low, bone-marrow-churning bass. Imagine the Bristol-born genre taking shape inside the electric dreams of the mid-1980s: the drums with a twitching hi-hat and thump have that low, unhurried weight, while the electronics give the space around them a cool, glassy clarity. After the movement of the preceding songs, this slower finish lets the record exhale. Its change of pace offers a place to sit with everything that has happened. Get Mean gives Matthews and Muller’s affection for post-punk, synthpop, goth, and dance music considerably more room to misbehave. They have grown as people, their lives have changed, and their music has had the good sense to evolve. Those expecting Pain on an endless loop, or Careful with a fresh set of track titles, may find this development inconvenient. For listeners who share Jae and Gus’s musical curiosity, there is pleasure in hearing them loosen up, follow their enthusiasms, and discover what this new chapter of their partnership can become. And if Get Mean isn’t the Boy Harsher you ordered, well, tough shit. Listen to Get Mean below and order the album here. Additional listening and purchase options are available here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Since forming in 2014, Matthews and Muller have taken Boy Harsher from the small cassette run of Lesser Man, whose Pain spread widely online, through Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their background in film became central to 2022’s The Runner, which they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their work in cinema also includes The Lonely Woman, their debut feature as directors, starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, and Sturgill Simpson. Boy Harsher’s The Heartbreak Tour resumes September 25 at Basilica Hudson, with North American dates running through November 5 at New York’s Knockdown Center. items.body: ケイシー・カンジェローシ 初来日リサイタルに寄せて 世界中のパーカッショニストを魅了する演奏家・作曲家、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その初来日リサイタルが、2026年9月26日（土）、長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県）で開催される。公演に寄せられた3人のコメントと映像から、その魅力を紹介する。 打楽器音楽の常識を覆す発想 新野将之（マルチパーカッショニスト） 僕が最も敬愛する打楽器奏者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。 彼の音楽には、「打楽器でここまでできるのか！」という驚きが詰まっています。卓越したテクニックはもちろん、タンバリンやスネアドラムの可能性を極限まで追求し、石を打ち合わせる音、電子音、パントマイムまで音楽の中へ大胆に取り込んでしまう。その発想は、まさに打楽器音楽の常識を覆すものです。 そして何より面白いのは、彼の音楽が「聴く」だけでは終わらないこと。音、身体、動き、空間……すべてをひとつの表現として融合させ、クラシック音楽の枠を飛び越え、新しいエンターテイメントへと昇華させていきます。 アートでありながら、圧倒的に楽しい。 知的でありながら、魂を揺さぶる。 打楽器の未来を切り拓いてきた開拓者、ケイシー・カンジェローシ。その唯一無二の世界を、ぜひ生で体感してください！ ﻿ 身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化 小室敬幸（音楽ライター） 1982年にアメリカで生まれたケイシー・カンジェローシは、打楽器を音だけでなく、奏者の身体や身振りまで含む舞台表現として捉えているユニークな打楽器奏者で作曲家だ。今回のリサイタルで演奏されるティエリー・ドゥ・メイ《Silence Must Be!》は、その志向を象徴する選曲である。メイはローザスを率いるアンヌ・テレサ・ドゥ・ケースマイケルら、ベルギーのコンテンポラリーダンスと密接に活動し、音楽的にはルイ・アンドリーセンらに連なるヨーロッパ的なミニマリズムを結びつけた作曲家。そのメイのような音楽の系譜に位置づけられるカンジェローシは、代表作《Meditation No.1》を含む自身の作品でも、打つ、振る、構えるといった動作や反復が、音と同じほど重要な表現になる。ダンスや演劇に通じる身体表現と、超絶技巧の打楽器演奏を一体化させており、今や世界中の若いパーカショニストを魅了している作曲家なのだ。目で見て真価が味わえる音楽なので、日本で初めて行う本格的リサイタルは必聴・必見である！ フィクションとフィジカルのあわい 加藤綾子（ヴァイオリニスト） YouTubeやInstagram上で切り抜かれる、カンジェローシの身体。バストアップであったり、手元や指先であったりするそれらを画面越しに見たとき、わたしたちは、まずそのディテールに心を奪われる。その身体は多彩な楽器を、ごく当たり前に扱う（ように見える）。ティエリー・ドゥ・メイのスコアを、美しく実現する。石ころもオルゴールも、スティックも、あまりに自然に振る舞うものだから、まるでオブジェクト・シアターを鑑賞しているような感覚に陥る。 そのうえで、彼は切実な演奏者であり続ける。鍛錬された身振りは、どこまでいっても彼自身あるいは他者の音楽を実践し、批評するためにある。その切実さが、きっと、ひとびとの全身を鷲掴む。画面越しではない、実存として長久手に立つ「カンジェローシ」は、音楽というフィクションとフィジカルのあわいを鮮やかに描き、突きつけてくれるだろう。──つまり、生で見るカンジェローシの演奏は、めっちゃすごくてやばいはず、ということです。 公演情報 ケイシー・カンジェローシ パーカッションリサイタル TENDRILS 2026年9月26日（土）16:00 長久手市文化の家 森のホール（愛知県） 公演詳細：https://bunkanoie.jp/archives/9250

items.body: Photo by Vins Pedata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. We had the chance to converse over email about his latest work, Der Saal tobt, realized under the Ervin Omsk moniker, published by Orange Milk. The interview was edited collaboratively with the artist. David Murrieta Flores (ACL): Hi Sven, could you please talk a bit about the Ervin Omsk project for readers who are unfamiliar with it? Sven Fritz (EO): Hi David, sure. Ervin Omsk is a pseudonym I’ve been using to release experimental electronic music since 2020. The name doesn’t actually have any special meaning; it’s simply an anagram of my two first names. The project began in 2018 with a few musical collages that were strongly connected to the idea of exploring an abstract painting or sculpture in a particular room—in other words, a very spatial approach, in which I combined diverse sounds from a modular system, field recordings, voice, and so on. Fortunately, Orange Milk was willing to release these tracks on tape in 2020, with artwork by Keith Rankin. In 2023, a second album, titled Schmalster Point, was released on vinyl, with artwork by Brenna Murphy. Now the third album, Der Saal tobt, is being released on tape and CD, with artwork by Lukas Schmenger. Ervin Omsk is currently one of several projects I’m working on. However, it’s the only solo project, and therefore also the most intense one. All my other projects are collaborative—for example, most recently with the French musician Amédée de Murcia. Together, we released an album in March on the Italian label Søvn. There’s also the Hui project, which I’m doing together with Johannes Schebler (Baldruin). An album has just been released on Jollies, and another one was released on Nonlocal Research last year. I’m also part of the artist collective Trickster, where I collaborate with other artists to realize scenarios in the sense of a Gesamtkunstwerk. My role here often involves musical performances lasting several hours and spread out over multiple days. All of my projects fall within the realm of experimental electronic music, and Ervin Omsk really benefits from the many experiences I’ve had working with all these other musicians. This applies not only to production, but also to the concerts I play as Ervin Omsk. These performances, however, are more like interpretations or improvised versions of the tracks I release. ACL: As the liner notes describe it, Der Saal tobt is mimicry of an orchestral body. Usually, we would understand such a body as mechanically efficient and well-coordinated, tuned and built through practice. However, the album understands it differently, and the result is slightly opposite: it’s a body that seems “unpracticed”. How do you understand the relationships between these bodies’ organs? How do you understand the differences between the modern, “well-oiled” orchestra and the album’s version of it? EO: I recently went to a concert where a chamber ensemble performed a piece that really moved me. At the same time, I realized that I actually didn’t really know what was going on. I have no academic background in this field. For example, I lack knowledge of music history and theory, notation, instrumentology, the roles within an ensemble, and so on. So I can only form a vague idea of what is happening in this music. I sense its dissonance, complexity, and openness; at times, it almost feels improvised. At the same time, I associate orchestral music with something highbrow and inaccessible. And that would be, so to speak, a different perspective from the outside. I generally have a rather ambivalent relationship with high culture, because it often caters to unchanging expectations and cultivates a kind of institutional sophistication. And in this context, the terms “efficient” and “coordinated” become interesting: these are actually very performance-oriented categories, which I would spontaneously associate with economics and sport. What do they have to do with music? But yes, an orchestra also needs this high degree of functionality, because, for example, it follows an idea or an order in the form of a notation. The musicians ensure that everything runs smoothly because they have mastered their instruments. To put it bluntly, we could argue that a modern, well-oiled orchestra must function—which sounds almost a bit cold and predictable. In music or art, however, I am not interested in categories like “well rehearsed,” “efficient,” and “coordinated” at first. It is rather the state outside these functions that moves me. To me, the intuitive and the seemingly contradictory have always been special qualities. There is, for example, that brief moment when an orchestra or a small ensemble tunes up. It is an undefined jumble of sounds, a wonderful moment of uncertainty. I am fascinated by the orchestra pit and its sound. But I come from a different musical background, both technically and culturally. I only play guitar, I can sing, and I know some things about synths and computer music. So I can’t imitate the orchestra; I can only bring electronic instruments into play, which then, through practice, become their own form of an orchestral body. And the interactions between the organs aren’t without tension; they sometimes get in each other’s way, and they don’t always speak the same language. And that’s what makes their relationships so special to me. There’s no oil here—more like sand in the gears and friction, to stick with your analogy. ACL: What is the process that you follow in order to craft a track? How do you understand the connections between tracks, once they are finished? EO: I can hardly describe it, really. There is no linear or additive process: each track is the result of countless intuitive decisions, right down to the smallest moments. I’m obsessed with details. The computer of course offers infinite possibilities and an overwhelming freedom. But that also means I usually can’t remember how the individual tracks were made. But I’ll try to describe it using the last track on the album as an example—which was actually the first track I produced: Right at the beginning, I made some very simple and short recordings of an alto recorder that I had borrowed from a friend and musician. After sampling and processing these recordings, the flute’s physical qualities were still there—the airiness, the directness, the softness, the hiss, and so on—but I could tune it freely and also control its overtones and noise, among other things. In fact, it suddenly seemed more like a symbol for an entire group of woodwind instruments or like an instrument that wanted to be several at once. And yet it still had something artificial about it. This impression was reinforced by the way it was played. Arpeggiators, whose tempo and rate were modulated by LFOs; animated envelopes that made glissandos possible; and the layering of several abstract flutes at once, varying only in their playing and sound. Then combined and blended with noises and glitches that picked up on the flutes’ patterns and intonations, countered them, and made them seem alien. Then it got a bit crowded, maybe like rush hour at the main train station. So then it was a constant process of sorting, resampling, stretching, compressing, cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and leaving pauses—until the track was finished. Something like that, very roughly. And as I said, there’s no single process that applies equally to all tracks. Other tracks have undergone several transformations. They were actually finished; then I completely rearranged them in the context of the entire album, because they didn’t feel right within the album’s dynamic, and the sequence of the tracks that unfolds over just 27 minutes. In addition, on this album I deliberately used certain sounds—such as the processed alto recorder— in several tracks, either obviously or just as a trace. And then, for me, all the pieces take place in the same space; they’re close and direct. Photo of Trickster setup by Sven Fritz. Courtesy the artist. ACL: What sort of gear do you use in this process? Thinking of gear less in terms of straightforward tools, and more socially in terms of extensions of your own thoughts and body, what does all this gear allow you to do? What does it inhibit you from doing? EO: I always try not to own too much gear. Even in production, I use only a few very specific and experimental tools so as not to unnecessarily expand the range of possibilities: a small modular system, MIDI controllers, Ableton Live, with digital samplers, sound generators, M4L devices, a few effects, and then a few flutes and microphones. I like the second part of your question. As a child, I played a home organ—two manuals, bass pedals. After that, I played electric guitar and sang for a long time, always in the context of bands. Vocals and guitar, in particular, are two very direct and physical instruments. It’s almost impossible to transfer that feeling to the world of synthesizers and computers, because playing them is less about gestures and more about fine motor skills involving the hands, fingers, eyes and ears: knobs, pads, trackpads, clicking, looking, listening and so on. But when it comes to abstract thinking about music, synthesizers and computers offer another advantage. They expand the scope of what I can imagine musically and put me in a constant state of learning and wonder. It’s sometimes like a rush. Surely also because I don’t understand everything. But in any case, it changes my own perception of sound, because these machines basically function like auditory microscopes. You can dive incredibly deep with your ears and your thoughts. ACL: Going back to the idea of orchestration, do you understand yourself as the orchestra’s director? Perhaps the orchestra itself, as an abstract embodiment? Perhaps the orchestra’s prompt-maker, to use contemporary code? In short – what is your own position within or without the orchestral body of the album? EO: A prompt-maker relies on clear codes or language as commands, right? That wouldn’t be immediate enough. And unfortunately, I don’t know much about the work of a conductor. But if I may set that aside for a moment, it might be something between a conductor and the orchestra itself. Here’s how I picture it: there’s a room full of objects, no musicians. So I rush through the ranks and set these objects into motion, sound, gestures, and relationships with one another. That would be very closely linked to experiences with live performances—both the role of the conductor and the abstract embodiment. Two examples: There’s this collective project called Trickster, which I’ve already mentioned: very irregularly, we realize a series of evenings as an image—no hierarchy, no stage, no beginning, no end, and thus no mood-setting service. In one of the those projects, I arranged 6–8 different speakers, several mixers, an electric guitar, a spontaneous choir of friends, several synthesizers, a percussionist, and two friends playing the French horn and the soprano recorder, spread throughout a room of about 100 square meters. Here, my role was more like that of a conductor who, over the course of about five hours, activated and collaged all of this using clear impulses and several loopers. Charging and discharging the space, playfully and improvisationally. Then recently I put together a live setup for some shows that had to fit into a backpack. A computer, two MIDI controllers, a small semi-modular synthesizer, and a microphone for vocals. Yet I prepared it in such a way that there were always five different instruments that I could play simultaneously. That was a bit demanding, but very direct, all on a small table—more as if I were many instruments, or, if you will, the orchestra itself. Turning knobs, playing pads, plugging in cables, tuning, singing, applying effects, controlling, not controlling. Photo by Matt Favero. Courtesy the artist. ACL: I’d like to return now to the question of mimicry – it’s an aesthetically loaded term, but it’s possible to contrast it with the idea that there is something organic to the body we are listening to in the album. If we understand the album’s body as more of an automaton, what are its possibilities/capacities/abilities when thinking about traditional musical categories of representation like “expression”? EO: Oh, that’s a really tough question, and I’m not sure I fully understand it. Mechanization could also be understood as a rigid and hierarchical process, but the automaton of the album feels alive to me. That would be more like a cyborg, right? But sure, let’s stick with the image of the automaton. I don’t think of it as a concrete thing with a particular physical form, but rather as an abstract machine, as algorithms and processes. In order to see what abilities it has in terms of traditional musical categories, I have to listen to it. So I’ll pretend for a moment that I didn’t build the automaton. At first, it sounds to me like a machine that seems to define its own form, processes, and movements, acrobatic and unpredictable, like a shapeshifter. It leads an inscrutable life of its own. The mistakes it makes are constantly incorporated into its search for form. A complex and delicate act. But only on the first, and perhaps the second, listening. Once you have become familiar with the complexity, the mechanisms, and the glitches, the form and nature of the automaton become clearer. Perhaps that is the moment when we can return to the “category of representation,” once we have understood the language of the automaton. Because “musical expression” may not be as organic, immediate, and human as we like to think. It is also part of a tradition and works through codes, conventions, expectations, and learned gestures—only seemingly self-evident. The automaton, of course, is only indirectly part of this tradition. In this logic, perhaps the ability of the automaton does not lie in “expressing” something in the classical sense, but in using, shifting, exaggerating, or also refusing these codes of expression. It maybe has the potential to transform many different sounds, instruments, gestures, figures, and experiments into a different but nevertheless familiar form of expression. And perhaps through its artificiality and distance it can make something audible that a human body would not do in this way. But the question really is very abstract. I hope I was able to give a somewhat meaningful answer here. Photo by Tobias Ullrich. Courtesy the artist. ACL: You did, thank you! Now, I’m interested in the meaning of the various track titles. There’s a playful overtone about things going wrong, failing in wholesome ways, or simply being the result of an essay in something (the “Memo Grisaille”, for instance, which alludes to the formative, practical painting made in shades of black or grey that emerged in the Renaissance). What links the process through which you made each track with the titles you chose for them? EO: Collecting titles or sentences is an independent process that I and other friends have been practicing since art school. I’m interested in titles because they add an associative layer to the individual track or the entire album. The album artwork by Lukas Schmenger does that too, by the way. Like the artwork, the titles are an important part of the album, even though they only come into the process at a later stage. I think the titles of the album relate in a certain way to its dynamics and moods. So I really associate the album title “Der Saal tobt” with an image of an agitated and unrestrained group of people. A feeling and sound somewhere between threat and excitement maybe. At the same time, it’s important for me to break up some kind of sonic overload with an everyday and blunt remark like “Beim besten Willen,” which rather expresses a refusal or incomprehension. So I also like the laconic quality of titles. With “Memo Grisaille,” though, it wasn’t my intention to trivialize this art-historical term. I simply like the combination of the words in terms of their sound, and the piece has something fragile and searching about it, like a memory that only becomes sharp and distinct in certain moments. So, with each title, there is an association that relates to the mood of the piece—with it or against it. ACL: Your previous album already explored a sense of joy derived from electronic sound interactions. Considering the track title themes, I think the argument can be made that there’s a humorous undercurrent in Der Saal tobt – there’s a philosophical perspective that says, basically, that it’s funny when things act like persons, but also the other way around. As the album’s automaton furiously fumbles around, we could be inspired to laugh: have you ever thought of experimental electronic music as possibly funny? Would you see a role for humor within your work, in the past, now, and in the future? EO: Experimental electronic music can be fun, sure. But so far, I haven’t gotten that feeling from this album. Then again, maybe I’m just missing something because I wasn’t sitting at the instruments or in front of the computer laughing while making it. Maybe it’s already fun when something unexpected happens. The staging of errors that make the automaton seem human, the unusual sounds, the friction in the gears, getting tangled up in the gestures—all of that could be interpreted as fun. For me, these are necessities, because I fear a well-oiled machine—and thus the predictable. And perhaps also I can’t take things, or myself, too seriously. So there may, after all, be a certain humorous distance, and therefore an unconscious influence on the tracks. But as the author myself, I can’t hear it. And that means humor would not have a defined role right now. If anything, it just happens, as it does in encounters with other people. For me, humor is indispensable there. In any case, I want to keep thinking about your question. There are quite a few inspiring examples in music, but also in visual art, that I would definitely describe as humorous. And maybe humor can get a more definite role in my work too. ACL: Thank you very much for your time, Sven. Is there anything else you’d like to tell our readers before closing this interview? EO: I’d like to thank you for these really challenging and intense questions. They went quite deep, and I found it very inspiring to think about them. Now I’m curious to know what it’s like to listen to the album after reading this interview—how it affects the way we perceive and contextualize this music. Especially since the album doesn’t necessarily need a strong conceptual framework, as it was created largely intuitively. Talking about it this way now almost feels like a kind of mental post-production, even though the music is already finished. And I consider it something special in itself to be able to release music like this, in the hope that there will be a few people out there who will actually listen to it and perhaps even find something in it. Thanks again for this opportunity.

An instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one OBA by OBA   Power up the hi-fi and get your favorite seventies era Sci-Fi laserdisc movie cued up on your vintage home entertainment system, turn the volume down on the film, and turn up the volume on OBA to let them provide the soundtrack. Turning the TV down and the stereo up is something old headz used to do. Out pattern making tendencies will find parallels with the visuals on the tube and the sounds from the music matching up in eerie ways. Look how far this took the acid addled minds of people who did this with the Wizard of Oz and the Dark Side of the Moon! OBA has provided an instant soundtrack to your inner movie, or your outer one. The project got started when three friends from three different continents found themselves in the same place and made a recording session, as musical friends are wont to do. The frequency wizard Amir Khay Nir from the USA, had met up with Orri Dror from Iceland, and Benjamin Esterlis in Israel. All of these fellows are multi-instrumentalists, making this an outing in overdubs after the initial recordings. But it is so freaking solid you think it was all happening live, and that’s the beauty of the recorded medium. It can make a live band out of a trio who live in far flung corners of the world. When I hear this music, I can see them playing, even it was completed after the initial sessions, and even if I don’t know what any of them look like. Synth’s swoon around drums, guitar and bass from the opening tones in an energetic weave. Not long after opening on “Ptaltalim” it starts to sound like a blurred VHS tape with bad tracking, but just for a second. The edited imperfection makes you awake to the perfection of the music, all moving into an action packed, almost aggressive soundscape of tight knit interlinking rhythms. What stands out: Intertwined souls: The chords and melodies played here make you know that you are listening to a group of people who are at ease musically syncing to each other despite the normal distances that separate them on the globe. We hear how the bass and guitar dialogues in pleasure with percolating synth, and whispers of flute as they paint the air and space and space with sound in a mood of sonic freedom. Emotional narrative: Though there is no voice and there are no lyrics in this entirely instrumental album, it moves naturally along an arc of action, reverie, intimation, and release across seven songs. It’s a soundtrack, but you make up the movie in your head. Chromatic resonance: From the melancholic power of “Luna Gal” to the electro-baroque impressionism of “Ketem” and progressive passages reminiscent of long time favorites such as Klaus Schulze, the album progresses like a well-structured musical short story (it’s a short and concise album) even as it permutates along the lines of something out of the studio of Gottfried Michael Koenig. Calculated chaos: All the notes are in the right place, and though there are a lot of notes, it’s not about showing off virtuosity. The skill of the players is in service to each composition. It’s a sincere work paying homage to classic forms, showing those forms are just as exciting when made anew. A touch of acid: Psychedelic inspiration is prominent throughout this work which invites dark room, eyes closed, introspective listening for out of body time. New listens reveal new textures, emotion and the craftsmanship that goes with attention to detail. OBA is available on Schwarz Neon Licht. items.body: The Dexadream seems to soar hundreds of miles above our atmosphere, while DFTSKZ-V333 drifts in and out of downtempo electronic bubbles of sound and space, funk, and textural, beat-laden wonders. Across both releases, Xurba folds left-field elements into a language entirely his own, shaping sound into something hazy, distant, and quietly otherworldly.   Suspended somewhere between memory and imagination A hauntological layer drifts through both DFTSKZ-V333 and The Dexadream, as elongated, slowly evolving loops—dark, buried, and scorched with abstraction—sees longtime fuzzy electronic sonic sculptor Will Brazier-Smith (aka Xurba) continuing to push ambient time capsules into unfamiliar territory. Where DFTSKZ-V333 settles into darker ambient motifs punctuated by subtle percussive bleeps, The Dexadream lifts that same hazy sensibility into a more expansive space, with atmosphere and downtempo noise conjuring a sense of nostalgic bewilderment. Much like the peculiar, roughened soundtracks of Pentagrams Of Discordia, Xurba blends, refines, and accents fragments into dreamlike ambient worlds that feel suspended somewhere between memory and imagination. The Dexadream seems to soar hundreds of miles above our atmosphere, while DFTSKZ-V333 hovers near terra firma—weaving in and out of downtempo electronic bubbles of sound and space, funk, and textural, beat-laden wonders. Across both releases, Xurba folds left-field elements into a language entirely his own, shaping sound into something hazy, distant, and quietly otherworldly. items.body: In a world increasingly obsessed with acceleration, Ekzon offers something altogether more radical—the opportunity to pause, listen, and feel the architecture of the moment dissolve gently into light. Spaces you can inhabit rather than simply observe Ambient Series Volume 2 by Ekzon   Ekzon maintains his high-calibre, sophisticated corner of sound and rhythmic creation with the stunning self-released Ambient Series Volume 2. Throughout my experience of ambient music’s more spacious possibilities, I have remained resolutely attached to the seminal 76:14 by Global Communication: another timestamp, and one of the first truly compelling ambient albums to emerge in the wake of The Orb‘s The Orb’s Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld, itself part of a lineage stretching back to Brian Eno‘s earliest explorations of spatial, aural atmosphere in Music for AIrports—these that became the seed of decades of an entire genre and beyond. This history lends some sense of the gravitas from which Ekzon operates—and perhaps unknowingly continues—in his own experiments with atmosphere as the leading texture. Already a deft hand at next-level rhythmic, programmatic glitch and electro-adjacent finery, this second collection extends those ideas across twelve tender pieces articulating contemporary urban life—not as a cold technological landscape, but as something lived within, felt through and quietly transformed by human presence. “Throughout all 12 pieces, multi-timbral pads drift through peaks and troughs of rhythmic puncture and oceanic blooms of turquoise transcendence.” ~Will Dawkins Titles and temperatures such as “Inertial Dream,” “A Quiet Ascent,” “Fading Echoes” and “City Lights” frame a subjective, phenomenological view of contemporary advancement, while the immediately captivating “Machines, Men, and Nature” feels almost like a small manifesto: a reconciliation of the organic and synthetic, the constructed and the instinctive. There is a generosity here, a willingness to let sound breathe rather than constantly announce itself. Throughout all 12 pieces, multi-timbral pads drift through peaks and troughs of rhythmic puncture and oceanic blooms of turquoise transcendence. Figurative angels seem to circle somewhere within the mix, gently worrying at the heartstrings without ever slipping into sentimentality. At times there are beats to grasp and solidify; at others, only clear air, the scent of magnolia, and beautiful collisions of earnest intention. The feeling of pragmatic melancholy that endures after the almost static movement in the exquisite “Twilight Water” is a not to be missed experience. Just stunning. Closing titles duties goes to the sublime “Crystallised” a breathtaking pulse of warm fogged out bliss in motion. Finally, for me, what makes Ambient Series V2 especially compelling, and adjacent to the aforementioned classics is its sense of unremitting balance, its relationship to its desire to be expressed. Ekzon understands that atmosphere need not mean inertia, and that sophistication need not sacrifice its correlation to necessary warmth. These tracks are spaces you can inhabit rather than simply observe: quietly detailed, emotionally open and touched by a rare sense of profound possibility. In a world increasingly obsessed with acceleration, Ekzon offers something altogether more radical—the opportunity to pause, listen, and feel the architecture of the moment dissolve gently into light. items.body: Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite Fictions by Lamasz & Grandbruit   Following release in early July, Fictions, somewhat mirroring its own dynamic, has taken time to reach peak resonance, creeping via auditory channels into psychoactive life, effectively bringing together the defining elements of each of Lamasz and Grandbruit into a single body of work. The return to Past Inside the Present of Pierre Luc (Lamasz) and Francis Tremblay (Grandbruit) with this collaboration comes on the back of four solo releases across the label: Fictions draws on Nature Morte (2020) and Broderie (2021) in tape loop-driven nature, Ruptures (2020) and Ville inerte (2021) in use of stratified guitar and environmental sound, common ground found in manicured noise, overall ambience and recursive habit. The brothers allow a gradual evolution, pieces looping into processed guitar-smeared harmonic tracts, tape hiss effectively taking on an active compositional role transcending background color. Expanding rather than merging the recognized individual styles of each, Fictions results in a chronostatic set of pieces with error honored as a hidden intention (see Eno’s Oblique Strategies) via analog processes, while holding to melodic virtues and economy of means. Fictions, then, adds to both artists’ growing back catalog, with languorous veiled melodies choreographed into an immersive suite with an emotional heft matching its timbral resonance. RIYL Chihei Hatakeyama, Rafael Anton Irisarri and artists in adjacent zones. items.body: Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance Disappear in Silent Ways by Halftribe   At the intersection of ambient, drone and environmental sound you’ll find Halftribe. His return to Dronarivm, Disappear in Silent Ways, comes in colors at once luminous and blurred, with a captivating ambi[val]ence, evoking a sense of moments presenting with past inside. Evanescence. This is achieved partly via a keen melodic sensibility with soft analog-y synths, field captures and odd voice fragments crafted into tone poems at once expansive and intimate. A form of minimalism runs through DiSW, manifest not in ideological stance but simple compositional practice; Ryan Bissett eschews the impulse for new entries to the sound stage for letting sounds evolve, adding color to broader canvas before letting in other elements. Sounds recede then return, revenant—a vague sense of movement over overt development; a soft ebb-flow dynamic, harmonic shifts emerging to color tenor, drones privileging depth over density, minute tonal shifts reframing space around and within. Melodic gestures emerge from drone surrounds—ground to figure, dissolving into field—drawing you in from perception’s margins, receding just as they seem to have settled. A site of refuge found after disappearing :: “Listen,” bids us attend to our environs, with its leitmotif ‘what we listen to is constantly feeding us’ adjuring mindfulness of what we let in. Field recordings bring in the natural world, as on “Dusk,” mixing layered drones with rainfall, evoking crepuscular horizons in day-night transition, inner-outer boundaries dissolved; or “Sanctuary,” pointing to a site of refuge found after disappearing; its oneiric mood feeds into “Yearn,” water flow enhancing a sense of peace through nature connection. “Windfall” shifts focus from water, distant whispers suggesting a field with grass and trees windblown, light filtering through branches to slow cloud drift. The title track brings an interlude of release, with birdsong and babbling before “Everything Comes to an End” leaves us with… that sense of evanescence. Following For the Summer, or Forever (2018) and Elegant, Golden (2022), Dronarivm has provided Halftribe with a platform to explore themes of presence, absence, removal and acceptance. The artist’s stamp, though, is more outline than full imprint, DiSW not looking to thematic statement so much as documenting the resonance of a feeling, in all its contours.
