items.body: Dudamel Conducts Prokofiev, Adams & Di Castri A visceral work headlined the opening program of the NY Philharmonic’s 2026-2027 season at Geffen Hall at Lincoln Center on September 16: John Adams’ On the Transmigration of Souls, a work written in response to the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center. As the 25th anniversary of the tragedy was just a few days prior, my gut was still tender from the echoes of the memories of that day. The work included a recording on which the names of some of the victims were spoken. Even a quarter century later, hearing the names put me right into that somber feeling I had experienced last week. The work effectively conveyed the desperation, shock and numbness, grief and sadness of those days. In a way, the orchestra provided a soundtrack for this actuality, and the overall effect was mystical, otherworldly and deeply affecting. At the conclusion, an exceptionally long “hang time” of silence hung over the concert hall – even after conductor Gustavo Dudamel lowered his arms, a visual signal that the piece was over, the audience stayed quiet, giving a bit of contemplative quiet before the roaring applause. I didn’t feel like hearing anything else after that – I just wanted to go to a bar and have a stiff drink. I was curious how the next piece, a world premiere by Zosha Di Castri, would land directly after the emotional tension of the Adams piece. Di Castri’s Invisible House — co-commissioned by the Philharmonic — opened with low brass and bass, a rumble that I felt in my chest. The Philharmonic’s brass had a starring role here, and the entire section sounded brilliant. The piece felt a little unfocused, although that could have been me — my head was still occupied with the sounds and emotions of Transmigration of Souls. The program closed with Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 5, and on this more familiar ground it was apparent how utterly terrific the Philharmonic sounded. Timbres of the various orchestral sections blended beautifully – achieving a very well-balanced sound. The symphony’s dark undercurrent showed off the winds especially well. Gustavo Dudamel‘s energetic conducting style was entertaining to watch as his entire body twitched and convulsed in the bombastic sections. In this concert, the New York Philharmonic sounded as good, and as present, as I’ve ever heard them. Finally, four years after Geffen Hall’s renovation, the orchestra has settled into the hall, and the hall has wrapped itself around the orchestra. Both the band and the space have gotten used to each other and found ways to work together as a single organism. The single was released on 21 August, composed and produced by the Hamburg musician Paul Lupa, who plays keyboards and bass and surrounds them with a live rhythm section: Big Finga on drums, Robert “Dubwise” Browne on guitar, Tribuman on horns. The horns carry the melodic line, the guitar marks the offbeat, and the vocal sits forward in the mix, with the phrasing of a lyric Macka B wrote himself, vocal melody included. What he tells the listener is to be who they are. Advice has been his line of work for forty years. He has been called “the Teacher” since the 1980s for songs about what to eat, how to look after yourself and how to treat other people, and the Wha Me Eat Wednesdays vegan raps he began posting in 2017 carried that voice far beyond the reggae circuit. Lupa has been building his Hamburg catalogue around Jamaican and German vocalists since 2022, and Macka B is the most established voice to record over one of his rhythms so far. items.body: “Yira Ye” takes its title from a Bambara phrase that means roughly “that’s how it is”, and it is the first single from L’Ombre du Croco, the debut album  Bamako Express release through Trad Records on 30 October. The Ghent quartet pairs two Belgian folk players, violinist Anouk Sanczuk and guitarist Florian De Schepper, with Malian balafonist and singer Joël Massa Diarra and Burkinabè percussionist Ousmane Dembélé on djembe and calabash. Their songs are sung in Bambara. Over the past year they have played concert stages and the balfolk nights of Flanders, where couples dance to live folk bands, and in 2026 they won Best Live Band at the Flanders Folk Awards. At a balfolk night the violin carries the tune for the dancers, and in Mande music the balafon does much the same job; “Yira Ye” passes the melody between the two over Dembélé’s djembe. The track moves from quiet melodic passages into full dance rhythm, and De Schepper steps forward for a guitar solo, recorded with the rest of the song by Jeroen Geerinck at Studio Trad. items.body: Ministry released “Singularity” on September 18, 2026 through Cleopatra Records, the third single from the industrial band’s final studio album, “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)“, due October 30. The track follows the earlier singles “Burned Out” and “We Hate” from the same record. “Singularity” takes on artificial intelligence, built around a warning voiced by a cyborg character: “Your time on this planet has passed […] we are in control.” A press release ties the song to recent public alarm over AI, describing it as Al Jourgensen and the band’s timely take on the subject. The music video was directed by Ben Garcia of Rage4Order Designs, working with Jourgensen and Joshua Bradford, a former Revolting Cocks bandmate who also directed the videos for “Burned Out” and “We Hate.” Where ‘Singularity’ sits on ‘Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)’ “Singularity” is track eight of ten. The album closes with “We’re Still Here”, the only track to feature former Ministry bassist Paul Barker, alongside the band’s current lineup of guitarists Monte Pittman and Cesar Soto, bassist Paul D’Amour, sampler and synth player John Bechdel, and drummer Pepe Clarke Magaña. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” arrives on vinyl, CD, cassette and digital formats, plus four vinyl variants (Green & Black Splatter, Silver & Black Splatter and Coke Bottle Green LPs) and two box sets pairing a splatter or marble LP with a picture LP, 7-inch and CD. Track seven, “The White Man Lied”, is left off the cassette and vinyl pressings. The full tracklist reads: Crickets Voices of Hate Clown Car We Hate Delete Grifter The White Man Lied Singularity Burned Out We’re Still Here (feat. Paul Barker) The album is available for preorder through Cleopatra Records. Ministry ‘Goodbye Europe’ tour dates 2027 Ministry closes out its career with a farewell touring cycle. Before the European leg, the band plays its remaining 2026 US and international dates: September 20 at Louder Than Life in Louisville, October 3 at the Salt Shed in Chicago, and October 24 at Sick New World Texas in Fort Worth, followed by Australia’s Good Things Festival in December with new side shows in Sydney and Adelaide. The “Goodbye Europe” tour, with Die Krupps as special guests, opens in Utrecht on April 2, 2027 and closes in Helsinki on May 1: April 2, 2027 – Utrecht, Netherlands April 3, 2027 – Saarbrücken, Germany April 4, 2027 – Brussels, Belgium April 6, 2027 – Manchester, UK April 7, 2027 – Dublin, Ireland April 9, 2027 – Nottingham, UK April 10, 2027 – London, UK April 12, 2027 – Paris, France April 14, 2027 – Madrid, Spain April 15, 2027 – Barcelona, Spain April 17, 2027 – Lausanne, Switzerland April 18, 2027 – Munich, Germany April 19, 2027 – Vienna, Austria April 21, 2027 – Prague, Czech Republic April 22, 2027 – Warsaw, Poland April 24, 2027 – Berlin, Germany April 25, 2027 – Hamburg, Germany April 26, 2027 – Copenhagen, Denmark April 27, 2027 – Oslo, Norway April 29, 2027 – Stockholm, Sweden May 1, 2027 – Helsinki, Finland A full US leg of the farewell tour has not yet been announced. About Ministry Ministry was formed in Chicago in 1981 by Al Jourgensen, a pioneering figure in industrial music. The project started with synth-pop material issued as four 12-inch singles on the newly founded Wax Trax! Records before the debut album “With Sympathy” on Arista Records in 1983. Jourgensen moved the band toward a harsher, sample-driven sound across “Twitch” (1986), “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989), then reached its widest audience with “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992), which brought the first of six Grammy nominations. Paul Barker played bass and co-produced through that period before leaving the band in 2003. Eight further albums followed before Jourgensen shut the band down in 2013. Ministry returned in 2018 with “AmeriKKKant”, then issued “Moral Hygiene” (2021) and “HOPIUMFORTHEMASSES” (2024), its 16th studio album. In March 2025 the band released “The Squirrely Years Revisited” on Cleopatra Records, a set of re-recorded songs from its early synth-pop catalogue, and followed it with first-ever official videos for “Everyday Is Halloween” and “I’ll Do Anything For You” and a Jurgen Engler remix of the live track “Dancing Alone” in March 2026. Alongside Ministry, Jourgensen has run Revolting Cocks, Lard, Pailhead and Surgical Meth Machine; Barker returned to recording as Lead Into Gold in 2023. Across 45 years, Ministry has released 17 studio albums, 8 live releases and 8 side projects, toured five continents, and published an autobiography and two documentaries. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” closes that catalogue as the band’s final album, and “Singularity” is its third single.

items.body: US goth-industrial artist EVA X released the single “Dance in Shadows” on 18 September 2026, alongside the announcement of her second album, “TURBOPINK”, due 6 November. The single mixes synthpop, metal, power pop and 80s-referencing production, and comes backed with a breakbeat remix by Stoneburner. “Dance in Shadows” was written by EVA X collaborator Gaby Gustafson after a co-worker and friend died of an aggressive form of cancer. “I had written a super sad song originally, but I knew she’d hate that. It was really important to her to find joy wherever she could. So I ended up reworking the track into Dance in Shadows, our happy little song about death,” Gustafson stated. The B-side carries a breakbeat remix of the track by Stoneburner. EVA X’s ‘TURBOPINK’ album due 6 November “TURBOPINK” follows EVA X’s debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, released on Distortion Productions in 2022. “Dance in Shadows” serves as the album’s preview single. EVA X returns with a full band for the touring cycle around the new record. About EVA X EVA X began as a bedroom producer, releasing her first tracks in 2019 and building a following in the goth and industrial scene through a fusion of synthwave, industrial, power pop and metal elements. Her debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, came out on Distortion Productions in 2022 and appeared on several “best of 2022” year-end lists. She has performed at New Jersey’s Dark Force Fest, Seattle’s Mechanismus Festival and Calgary’s Terminus. Side-Line previously covered her single and video “Dopamine Blind” (2024) and her video “Machine” (2021). With “Dance in Shadows”, EVA X previews her second album, “TURBOPINK”, out 6 November 2026.

items.body: Nick Rhodes of Duran Duran produced Wendy Bevan’s new single “Sleepwalkers,” the third preview of the UK goth electro-pop artist’s album “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18. The track pairs Bevan’s vocals with atmospheric synthesizer arrangements built around a feeling of loss without a clean goodbye, leaving the listener suspended between holding on and letting go. Bevan describes “Sleepwalkers” as a piece about two sides of the same uncertainty: “the old world that’s disappeared and the future that hasn’t arrived.” “We’re left somewhere, timeless and in between,” she said. “Sometimes we become so lost in our own dreams that we don’t see the destruction they cause, or recognize that we may be disappearing from our own lives.” On the song’s central tension, she added: “The act of not choosing can be just as violent as a bull in a china shop. While we long for a place called home, we unconsciously fill the spaces between with our own self-destructive behaviors.” “Sleepwalkers” is track nine on “Alone With The Unknown,” out September 18 on Chiaroscuro. The 13-track album, which also carries the bonus cut “Crazy Kinda Feeling,” was preceded by the singles “Innocence” in July and “Fragile Times” in August, both also produced by Nick Rhodes. The record continues Bevan’s production partnership with Rhodes, which began with the instrumental Astronomia series. About Wendy Bevan Wendy Bevan is a British singer, violinist and photographer raised in London who now lives in Los Angeles. She released the single “Love from the Moon” via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2016, alongside a parallel career as a fashion and fine-art photographer. In 2018 she began collaborating with Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes, working between Los Angeles and London, on a series of cinematic instrumental compositions released from 2021 as the Astronomia project through Tape Modern, the label founded by Stephen Duffy and Nick Rhodes. The series opened with “The Fall of Saturn” on the spring equinox of 2021, followed by “Astronomia II: The Rise of Lyra” that June. In October 2024, Bevan released “Chromesthesia,” a five-track instrumental album, through her own Bandcamp page. She and Rhodes then returned to song-based material for “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18, with “Sleepwalkers” as its third single.

About Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection is one of several recording names used by Slovak producer Alexander Borsov, alongside Dark the Keeper, Darkmechanic and Stellar Dynamics, all mixing electro-industrial, noise and horror-themed dark electro elements. Borsov is also a member of the group Diverje and got his start in metal bands including Morgue, Atom, Cremation Deads, Sarcoma and Satura before moving into electronic production. Under the Ghost Reflection name, Borsov released the album “Dark Thinker” in June 2022 and the single “Dark Noise” in February 2024. “Dark Triad” followed in September 2025 and is now released digitally through Aliens Production, the Slovak dark electronics label that has operated since 1997 and hosts a roster of industrial, dark electro and EBM-adjacent acts.

items.body: Union Chapel in London stages “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” on 4 November 2026, a one-off return of Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent’s “Vinyl Requiem” to the venue where it premiered in 1993. Doors open at 18:30 and the programme starts at 19:30. Tickets are £18 plus booking fee through gigantic.com and are on sale now. The evening also marks the launch of a limited-edition double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem” on Touch, the label Jeck was signed to from 1995 until his death in 2022. Vinyl Requiem 33.3 event details The programme centres on a full-scale projection of the 55-minute edited film of the 1993 performance, followed by a Q&A with people connected to the work and to Jeck’s creative life: Ghislaine Boddington (artistic director of the arts collective shinkansen), Mary Prestidge and Lol Sargent, the visual artist who created “Vinyl Requiem” with Jeck. Jon Wozencroft, co-founder of Touch, is also billed to take part. All profits from the night go to The Philip Jeck Foundation, a charity set up by Jeck’s family after his death to fund artists who produce experimental and creative work. Conceived by Jeck and Sargent at the start of the 1990s under the working title “The Death of Vinyl”, “Vinyl Requiem” was built for the 1993 Union Chapel performance from an 8-by-6-metre wall of 180 white Dansette record players, combined with 9 slide projectors and 2 16mm film projectors, according to Touch’s own catalogue notes. Three “Dansette operators” walked platforms in front of the record-player wall to swap discs live during the piece. The 1993 premiere was staged with the Institute of Contemporary Arts and also travelled to Ghent’s Time Festival in Belgium, later touring the UK, Austria and Belgium with support from the Arts Council. It won the Time Out Performance Award for Best Site-Specific Event in 1993. Sargent described the piece’s intent in an interview given around the time of its 20th anniversary: “What Philip and I created was an abstract expressionistic performance made in a very intuitive way to celebrate over 100 years of the mass public experience of the ‘record’. It was an art installation performance about a medium, using the medium.” Jeck, discussing the same period, was careful to separate the piece from nostalgia: “[Vinyl Requiem was not] a big mourning for records, I am not anti CD. It is a good starting point to mark this time of change from vinyl to other formats.” He also drew a direct line between his own practice and Sargent’s: “Lol uses his computer-controlled projectors as paint brushes. He paints with light which is similar to the way that I work with sound.” The critic David Toop, writing about the piece at the time, described its atmosphere in a short, often-cited line: “a mood of poignancy. Perhaps sadness is intrinsic to the medium.” About Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent Philip Jeck was born on 15 November 1952 and studied visual arts at Dartington College of Arts in Devon. After a trip to New York in 1979 introduced him to DJs including Walter Gibbons and Larry Levan, he began building compositions from old record players and vinyl in the early 1980s, initially scoring work for dance and theatre companies, including a five-year collaboration with choreographer Laurie Booth. “Vinyl Requiem”, made with Sargent for the 1993 Union Chapel performance, became his best-known work. Jeck signed to Touch in 1995 and released a run of albums on the label including “Loopholes” (1995), “Surf” (1998), “Stoke” (2002), “7” (2003), “Sand” (2008), “An Ark for the Listener” (2010) and “Cardinal” (2015). “Sand” was named the second-best album of 2008 by The Wire. He received the Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award for Composers in 2009. Jeck also collaborated with Jah Wobble, Jaki Liebezeit, David Sylvian, Janek Schaefer and Gavin Bryars, among others; his final credited recording was “Stardust”, a 2021 collaboration with Faith Coloccia. He died on 25 March 2022 in Liverpool, aged 69, following a brief illness. His family, including Mary Prestidge, subsequently established The Philip Jeck Foundation in his name. Lol Sargent is a UK visual artist who worked with Jeck on “Vinyl Requiem” from its conception, designing and hand-triggering the piece’s slide and film projections during live performances. He later oversaw the archival 55-minute edit of the 1993 film, released on DVD in 2013 with all proceeds going to The Philip Jeck Foundation. “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” reunites Sargent with the venue, the film and several of the people who worked on the original production, alongside the new Touch double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem”.

items.body: Unter Strøm, the electronic duo of Alex Gonzales (Matte Blvck) and John Kunkel (The New Division, John Grand), release Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase, an independent live recording that runs a little over 84 minutes. The set documents a full Unter Strøm performance at a Breathing Records showcase and includes live versions of “Fragment” and “Stumbling” performed before either track had been released, along with several vocal tracks the duo were still developing. Unlike the project’s prior singles, “Transmission 003” is not a studio release. It is a concert recording, filmed and uploaded to YouTube, capturing the duo’s first time performing an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience. Unter Strøm test unreleased material in a live setting The showcase gave Gonzales and Kunkel their first chance to hear the project’s unreleased catalog through a full sound system and gauge a crowd’s reaction to it in real time. Kunkel described the goal behind the set: “We wanted the set to present a broad landscape of the Unter Strøm sound and show how many different places the project can go. After working on this music for over a year, it was exciting to finally experience it through a proper sound system and watch people respond to it in real time. What makes it even more exciting is that we still have a lot more in the tank that didn’t make it into the set.” Gonzales, describing what the performance meant for the duo, added: “The Breathing Records showcase was the first time we played an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience, so it felt like an important moment for us. We performed an hour and a half of entirely unreleased material, including ‘Fragment’ and ‘Stumbling’ before either song had been released, as well as several vocal tracks that we were still developing. It gave us a rare opportunity to test this body of work in a live environment and see which moments connected instinctively with the audience.” About Unter Strøm Unter Strøm is an electronic duo formed by Alex Gonzales and John Kunkel, based between Los Angeles and San Diego after years of the pair working together in earlier bands and studio sessions. The project mixes techno, melodic house and industrial electronics. Gonzales also records as Matte Blvck, the San Diego-based darkwave and industrial trio he leads with Bidi Cobra and Daniel Corrales, whose releases include “Vows,” “Pupula Duplex” and “Soulless.” Kunkel is the Los Angeles-based producer and songwriter behind The New Division, the synth-pop project he has led since the 2000s, is part of the Los Angeles group Trade Secrets, and also produces melodic house as John Grand, an alias that has appeared on Armin van Buuren’s A State of Trance and on Above & Beyond’s Group Therapy Radio. Unter Strøm debuted in 2025 with the two-track single “Breathing” before signing to Breathing Records, the label that launched with the “Inhale Vol. I” compilation in November 2025. The duo then released “Orynth” on May 15, 2026, “Fold” on June 12, 2026, “Fragment” on July 24, 2026 and “Stumbling” on August 28, 2026, the four singles that made up the “Between Forms” run. “Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase” now documents the live set where “Fragment” and “Stumbling” were first performed, ahead of their studio releases, alongside new vocal material the duo have yet to put out.

items.body: The 21st-anniversary triple-vinyl reissue of Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” has a new release date of December 4, 2026, according to the Erasure Information Service newsletter sent to subscribers on September 18, 2026. The accompanying 12″ vinyl single, “Love Oneself” / “Delicious”, is now scheduled for November 20, 2026. The Andy Bell reissue was previously delayed after audio issues were found in the test pressings. Newsletter editor Richard Evans wrote that the issues have since been corrected, new test pressings are due shortly, and the release has been rebooked into the pressing plant’s production queue. Stock delivered ahead of the release date will be dispatched to fulfil pre-orders as soon as it arrives. Everyone who has pre-ordered Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” through Lexer Music will receive an MP3 version of the album while they wait, an offer that also applies to pre-orders placed via Lexer before September 28, 2026. The same MP3 offer applies to pre-orders of the “Love Oneself” / “Delicious” 12″ single. Vince Clarke contributes to new Ultravox book The same newsletter carries a mention of Vince Clarke‘s contribution to “Looking Backwards Towards The Future: The Story of Ultravox”, a book by Richard Evans due out on October 8, 2026 everywhere except North America, Australia and New Zealand, where it follows in February. Clarke was interviewed for the book about his fondness for Ultravox‘s “Systems Of Romance” album. The book is written with the cooperation of Ultravox’s surviving core members, carries a foreword by Moby, and includes additional contributions from Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes and producer Steve Lillywhite. Signed and dedicated copies are available to order through Lexer Music. Unofficial remix and a teased new chapter The newsletter also points to a new unofficial remix of Erasure’s “Stay With Me” by an artist called Klaak, posted to YouTube, following an earlier unofficial Klaak remix of “Hideaway”. The remix is not sanctioned by Erasure, Andy Bell or Mute. Evans also teased that preparations are underway to announce “the next exciting chapter in Erasure’s story,” tied to a forthcoming new Erasure album project. About Erasure and Andy Bell Erasure are the English synth-pop duo of Andy Bell and Vince Clarke, formed in London in 1985. Clarke had previously co-founded Depeche Mode and Yazoo, and formed The Assembly, before pairing with vocalist Bell to form Erasure. The duo built a run of UK and international hits through the late 1980s and 1990s, including “Sometimes,” “A Little Respect,” “Chains of Love,” “Blue Savannah” and “Always.” Erasure’s catalogue has been the subject of ongoing reissue campaigns, including a 2024 vinyl reissue push covering ‘Tomorrow’s World’, ‘Snow Globe’ and ‘The Violet Flame’, and the duo marked 40 years of “Who Needs Love Like That” in 2025. Bell has maintained a solo career alongside Erasure, releasing the album “Ten Crowns” in 2025 and continuing to perform and record under his own name; “Electric Blue,” now reaching its 21st-anniversary vinyl reissue, is among his earlier solo releases. Clarke has continued to work outside Erasure as well, contributing to and remixing for other artists’ projects, including Doublespeak, his covers collaboration with Blancmange, announced earlier in 2026. The Erasure Information Service newsletter, edited by Richard Evans, has served as the duo and Bell’s primary direct fan-communication channel for reissue updates, solo activity and, as of this newsletter, hints toward a new Erasure album project still to be formally announced.

items.body: Cocteau Twins released their fifth studio album, “Blue Bell Knoll,” through 4AD on 19 September 1988. Capitol Records licensed the record from 4AD for North America, making it the first Cocteau Twins album to receive major-label distribution in the United States. The dream pop album turns 38 this year. Vocalist Elizabeth Fraser named the album after Bluebell Knoll, a peak in southern Utah. Guitarist Robin Guthrie produced the record and handled keyboards along with synth and drum machine programming, while Simon Raymonde played bass and keyboards. All ten tracks are credited to Fraser, Guthrie and Raymonde: the title track, “Athol-Brose,” “Carolyn’s Fingers,” “For Phoebe Still a Baby,” “The Itchy Glowbo Blow,” “Cico Buff,” “Suckling the Mender,” “Spooning Good Singing Gum,” “A Kissed Out Red Floatboat” and “Ella Megalast Burls Forever.” Fraser sang the whole album in her own constructed language. Raymonde later described the sessions as a settled period for the trio: “it really felt like a period of creativity and freedom, we were all getting on great musically and socially, Liz and Robin were about to have a baby, I was about to get married, there was lots of joy around. Very productive! It was a really fun record to make.” Fraser connected that ease to the decision to drop conventional lyrics, telling The Quietus in 2017: “I gained so much from [inventing language] […] Writing Blue Bell Knoll I had a wonderful freedom to put lyrics aside and not to worry [about people’s opinions].” The album reached number 15 on the UK Albums Chart and number 109 on the US Billboard 200, and “Carolyn’s Fingers” climbed to number two on the US Alternative Airplay chart. Promotional videos accompanied “Carolyn’s Fingers” and “Cico Buff.” The vinyl edition came in a limited gatefold sleeve, and the album was the first 4AD title issued commercially on DAT. After 4AD reclaimed the North American rights to its back catalogue, Guthrie remastered “Blue Bell Knoll” for a 2003 reissue, and the album was repressed on 180g vinyl in 2014. It streams on Spotify. About Cocteau Twins Cocteau Twins formed in 1979 in Grangemouth, Scotland, around guitarist Robin Guthrie and bassist Will Heggie, who took the band name from a song by fellow Scots Simple Minds. Guthrie met Elizabeth Fraser in Falkirk in 1981 and asked her to sing. The group signed to 4AD and issued its debut album, “Garlands,” in 1982, followed by “Head over Heels” in 1983. Heggie left that year and Simon Raymonde replaced him, arriving in time for 1984’s “Treasure.” Two albums came in 1986: “Victorialand,” recorded largely as a duo while Raymonde worked on This Mortal Coil, and “The Moon and the Melodies,” a collaboration with ambient composer Harold Budd. “Blue Bell Knoll” followed on 19 September 1988 and became the band’s first record to enter the US Billboard 200, a direct result of the Capitol licensing deal. “Heaven or Las Vegas” arrived in 1990 and closed the group’s run on 4AD; Cocteau Twins then signed to Fontana for “Four-Calendar Café” (1993) and “Milk & Kisses” (1996), and disbanded in 1997. All three have kept working since. Side-Line covered Raymonde’s Bella Union label presenting the debut album by his project Lost Horizons in 2017, Guthrie’s ‘Riviera’ EP in 2021 and his ‘Springtime’ EP in 2022, and reported that Fraser had returned with her first new material in 13 years in 2022. “Blue Bell Knoll” turns 38 this year, the record that opened the American market to the band two years before its 4AD run ended.

items.body: Parissior is a Spanish project founded by DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. With “Human Control”, he releases his debut album, featuring ten tracks (although the vinyl edition contains only eight). While several EPs were released previously, this album consists entirely of new material, exploring themes such as digital identity, illusion, authenticity, and human imperfection. Musically, this translates into a very solid mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. The basslines sound menacing and pure EBM, while the kicks reveal clear Techno influences. There are also a few additional influences, such as Acid sequences, as well as some delightful old-school Techno elements that remind me of the Frankfurt scene of the 1990s. The way everything is put together sounds intelligent and, naturally, highly dancefloor-oriented. There are also some vocals worth mentioning, including a track featuring guest vocalist Jorge Tornin, although the vocals are not necessarily the most striking aspect of the album. “Human Control” is a very strong release that delivers a perfect blend of nostalgic moments and a more contemporary sound, in which Dark-Techno and EBM are inseparable and form a powerful cocktail. An album you absolutely must discover! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Eco Machines”: Eco Machines by Parissior About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly with the Espacio Cielo label, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control” is his first full-length album.

items.body: All the things I’ve seen, all the things I’ve been must upset you. Moving to a new city after a broken heart requires a certain faith in geography. Surely a different address, unfamiliar faces, and a few hundred miles can improve upon the person who packed the suitcase. Then comes the stranger discovery: the life you once wanted has become difficult to remember. Berlin’s Pretty Average explores that uneasy freedom on All I Wanted, I Forgot, a song about starting over and finding that some of your most cherished desires have quietly missed the connection. That uncertainty carries into the accompanying video, where performance footage blurs beneath layers of static and bleeding color, matching the disorientation of the band’s beautiful blur of shoegaze, post-punk, and alternative rock. One of the earliest songs Pretty Average wrote together, All I Wanted, I Forgot appears on the album The Highs and Lows of Being Pretty Average, released on cassette this past May. A cascading drumbeat sets the song in motion while sustained guitar notes spread across a dense bed of distortion. The bass carries a melodic ache familiar from The Cure, giving the guitars something solid to stretch against. There is a sweet sadness here that recalls the distance and desolation of Joy Division, though the broadening shoegaze textures allow a softer, almost yielding quality into the music. Candy’s voice sits low in the mix, as though she is singing from the next room and leaving the door closed. That separation gives the words their peculiar weight. The lyrics inventory experiences, former selves, prayers, and departures, addressing someone who might resent everything that happened beyond their reach. By the time that accounting reaches “All I wanted, I forgot,” even the original wish has become elusive. As the guitars swell, their accumulating layers suggest water moving across an inscription, gradually making the names and promises harder to read. Forgetting carries its own small mercy, along with the disquiet of losing something you once thought essential. The band describes the song as an exploration of “the disturbing yet exciting feeling of being in a new city and starting over with a wounded heart, leaving behind your past and your dreams.” Their conclusion is brief enough to sound almost surprised: “Somehow we became someone new.” The video gives that uncertainty a physical form. Blue and violet stage lighting washes over the musicians while overlapping images, colour separation, and television static repeatedly interfere with the view. Faces and instruments become difficult to hold in focus; a close-up gives way to another image before either quite settles. The effect suggests a concert being recalled through an unreliable recording, with the band’s presence surviving all the visual interference. It suits a song in which the feeling remains clear even as its original object slips away. Watch the video for All I Wanted, I Forgot below: Formed in Berlin in 2022, Pretty Average centre Candy’s perspective on identity, social rejection, and the uncertain prospects facing her generation. Their 2024 EP, All I Wanted, was produced by Francisco Parisi of Minimal Schlager, with a Musicboard Berlin scholarship following that year. Regular Berlin performances, a Spanish tour, and support slots with acts including Genn, DVTR, Francis of Delirium, and Adult DVD helped develop a project whose priorities remain rooted in playing together. Those priorities took some recovering. Lineup difficulties and disagreements with their former label delayed an album originally intended for 2025; the band credits a European tour this May with renewing their enthusiasm. Recorded in a self-made studio, The Highs and Lows of Being Pretty Average preserves the energy and imperfections of musicians sharing a room. Its extended songs also reflect their stated preference for small venues, direct support, and giving an album room for long songs and changes of pace. The album is available on cassette through Bandcamp and at the band’s concerts. Listen to All I Wanted, I Forgot below and purchase the single here. items.body: My backup earbuds are an aged pair of shitty blue Raycons someone gave to me years ago (probably because they too realized how shitty they are). The audio quality is terrible and whenever you reconnect them too many times or pause whatever you’re playing too often they start cutting out, and when you hold the button down to turn them off the left one makes this horrific lobit yelping noise that would probably burst your eardrum if you had it in your ear. It might be the worst thing I’ve ever heard, so naturally I’m obsessed with it. It’s not just the volume or the piercing frequency register but also the digital brutality of it, overclocked cheap circuitry screaming from its own kind of hell. Berlin-based artist Diego Behncke plumbs the depths of that hell with Teleplasty: Implex!, a pair of extended recordings performed live using a custom processing system (“consisting of optimal transport–based spectral morphs between recordings of chaotic synthesis via recursive nonlinear feedback”… yeah, sounds like hell to me). It’s the ugliest music he’s released yet; less second updates (2017) on his own Prensa Manual imprint had moments of beauty, and Severe Chronotopic Leakage (2024), though similar in approach, doesn’t lean into fractured fidelity. The code rips spectra to ribbons and whirls them in an algorithmic wind tunnel, whittling the already jagged edges of raw data samples to razor-sharpness. Listen on speakers if you can—the stereo slicing leaves open wounds in the air. “(II / ‘Pt. 8’)”, the newer of the two pieces, adds generated speech to the source soup, resulting in some uncanny moments that sound like robotic mumbling gargling. “Pt. 6” has a narrower textural range and feels almost tactile. Behncke envisions the human operator of his systems as a “regulator” rather than a performer, an intentional restriction that “tries to make flat issues of agency, proficiency, improvisation, or experience.” The key word there is “tries.” The innate constraints and autonomy of the materials certainly limit options, but the regulator must always make conscious decisions—even if they decide not to regulate at all. And on the other end, listeners also must decide who or what is responsible for the things we’re hearing. I, for one, choose to blame Behncke for the brief, ambiguous flashes of old organic friends: dynamic contrast, call and response, visceral intrigue. When it comes to recorded sound, someone is always complicit.

items.body: On " Chant ", another sculptor of silence shows her art. The magician is Magda Mayas, whose explorations of the outside and inside of her piano keeps astonishing us, including her inventiveness to create unheard sounds. Mayas is not only a musician, but also an academic researcher with several publications to her name, getting her PhD on the subject of " Orchestrating Timbre – Unfolding Processes of Timbre and Memory in Improvisational Piano Performance" (2019/20), which examines improvisation through timbre, space, movement, objects, and listening. I'm adding a few videos here to show her art. The first is an exercise that Magda Mayas developed for the Hochschule Luzern called " Thinking Silent Matter ". The excercise focuses on improvisation in a large ensemble context, bringing attention to silence and reduced sound material with slowly changing parameters, starting with the relevant quote : "... silence not only as absence of sound, but also silence as part of the sound" . In the video she guides her students through the concept of the exercise. Indeed, silence matters. It is even essential to anything we hear, whether we are aware of it or not, so why not actively use it in music? On the tree pieces of the album, she shows this in very different formats. The first and last piece were recorded in Australia, with two years apart, the middle track was recorded in Berlin in Tony Buck's Brief Sand Studio. The opening track, “ Embodied ,” recorded live at the SoundOut Festival in Canberra in February 2025, establishes its language through restraint. The piano notes arrive slowly, and the silences between them are as significant as the sounds themselves. Rather than functioning as a conventional prelude, however, this spaciousness becomes the central compositional device. Against the sparse piano framework, elusive sounds emerge from objects and tools used to activate the strings, producing a shifting field of resonance whose sources remain deliberately indistinct. The music is notably sparse, but never static; its intensity lies in the sustained concentration with which each sound occupies the space. “ Halcyon ” extends this approach while pushing the sonic material into considerably harsher territory. Carefully paced piano chords are subjected to feedback from a guitar amplifier, alongside a guitar pickup and various other objects. The amplification and feedback transform the piano’s familiar timbre, extending each chord into a dense, sustained resonance. Despite the expanded textural palette, the harmonic language remains remarkably focused: pitches occupy a restricted register and coalesce around a clear tonal centre. This tension between harmonic simplicity and increasingly abrasive resonance gives the piece its mesmerising quality. Developed in 2023 during the Harringtons Lane artist residency in New South Wales, “ Chant ” approaches the piano from yet another angle. The piece’s playback was recorded on sixteen different pianos, foregrounding variations in tuning and the subtle differences between instruments. Its structure is deceptively simple, built around the quiet repetition of two chords whose minute variations in tuning and timbre continually alter their perceptual weight. The effect is both soothing and strangely intense. Through repetition, small shifts become magnified, turning what might initially appear static into something constantly in flux. Across these three works, there is a consistent interest in reducing musical materials to their essentials while expanding the possibilities of resonance, texture and perception. The music derives much of its power from this paradox: the means are often minimal, yet the listening experience is anything but. What emerges is an aesthetic that feels simultaneously rigorous and intuitive—fresh, inventive and deeply attentive to the physical properties of sound. The title piece was also performed by Mayas at Roulette, streamed live on 30 Apr 2024. The video gives a great insight in her music but also on the added ingredients in the interior of her piano, things you can assume when you see a concert, but can usually at best only guess at. items.body:
Eight years can change a lot. For Khalid, it has meant new albums, new stories, a stronger sense of self, and perhaps most noticeably when he steps onstage, a newfound confidence.

The multi-platinum singer-songwriter first broke through with 'Location', released just before his high school graduation, before establishing himself with American Teen and its coming-of-age anthem 'Young Dumb & Broke'. Since then, his catalogue has grown to include Free Spirit, Sincere, and most recently After the Sun Goes Down, while collaborations with the likes of Billie Eilish, Normani, Halsey, Marshmello, and Benny Blanco have further expanded his reach across pop and R&B.

Now, Khalid is preparing to reconnect with Singapore fans at It's Always Summer Somewhere Tour on 24 November at The Star Theatre, presented by Live Nation Singapore. The show marks his first performance in the country since 2018, following a planned 2020 return that did not go ahead because of the pandemic.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

For Khalid, that long absence only means he has more of himself to share this time around.

“It's incredible,” he tells Bandwagon. “To be able to come back to a place that is so, so far from where I've grown up, where I originally live, I think is amazing. It really shows the power of music and just how far I can travel.”

There is also a touch of disbelief that so much time has passed.

“I'm even apologetic for taking so long to come back. Eight years is so long. So much life has happened since then, but it means that I have just more stories to bring with me when I come.”

A more confident Khalid

Fans who were there for Khalid's previous Singapore show might recognise the songs, but the person performing them has changed.

Asked what would surprise returning concertgoers most, Khalid doesn't point first to elaborate production or a new arrangement. Instead, he talks about confidence.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

“I feel like before I might have been a little bit more timid, a little bit more shy,” he says. “And I feel like now I feel a little bit more confident in my craft, in my voice.”

That confidence translates physically, too. Today's Khalid dances more. He jumps more. And despite being eight years older, he says performing somehow makes him feel younger than before.

“I have a lot more energy, a lot more life,” he shares. “It's so interesting because I'm older than I was before, but in a way I feel so much younger than the last time that I was on that stage.”

For an artist whose music has long documented growing up in real time, that evolution feels fitting. Sincere explored the emotions that come with getting older, while After the Sun Goes Down pushed Khalid into another musical chapter through a blend of R&B, electro-pop, and ’80s-inspired synths.

The result is a live show that allows him to put that growth in front of the same listeners who may have grown alongside him.

“I'm just excited to really show my audience growth,” he says.

Soundtracking a Singapore night

The Singapore stop is expected to span Khalid's catalogue, from 'Location', 'Better', and 'Talk' to collaborations such as 'Love Lies' and 'Eastside', alongside songs from his latest chapter.

But if one After the Sun Goes Down track had to soundtrack a night out in Singapore, Khalid already knows his pick: 'Momentary Lovers'.

“I just think that the song feels very electric, and it just reminds me of nights that I've had in Singapore, just nights that I've had myself,” he says. “And I really love that song so much, and it's a fun one.”

For all the new music and personal growth, however, one of his earliest hits still holds a special place in the live experience.

If Khalid could leave the stage and join his own audience for just one song, he would choose 'Young Dumb & Broke'.

“I would love to be one of my fans when I'm experiencing that song for the first time, or maybe even the third, second, fourth, however many times,” he says.

The reason is simple: there is an energy around the song that even Khalid, from his position at the centre of the room, can feel taking over.

“It takes over me on the stage,” he explains. “So I would love to experience that song, if I could, from a fan's perspective.”

Perhaps that desire says as much about Khalid's relationship with his music as anything else. Nearly a decade into a career that has taken his songs around the world, he is still curious about what they feel like from the other side of the barricade.

Come as you are

As for what Singapore fans should wear to the show, Khalid isn't interested in imposing a complicated theme.

“My dress code is: wear whatever makes you feel comfortable,” he says. “I'm a big believer in, you know, come as you are.”

It is an invitation that reflects how he sees his audience: not as one uniform fandom, but as a collection of different people who have found something of themselves in his songs.

“What I love about my audience is there are so many different types of listeners and types of fans,” Khalid says.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

And with a tour called It's Always Summer Somewhere, practicality helps.

“Feel free, feel loose. Wear something you can dance in, you can move in, you're not afraid to sweat in,” he adds. “But, you know, be you.”

Eight years after his last Singapore performance, Khalid isn't returning as the same artist who left. There is more confidence, more movement, more music, and, as he puts it, more stories.

For fans who have been waiting all this time, that might be precisely the point.

Although we are tiny, beautiful things often come in small packages, and size doesn’t diminish our place or importance in the grand scheme of things: we are special, precious, breathing into the cosmic wonder of the Universe and sharing in its majesty, a part of a chapter in its ongoing story. As Norvik says, ‘there is value to being humbled’, and the piano melodies are enraptured by the space in which we live. Atoms coalesce, eventually forming the biggest stars and growing like seeds to forge a blossoming Galaxy, of which there are billions and counting; where stars hang like stationary snowflakes, pinned to unending black. Chan’s piano melodies are just as precious. Each one lights up like a star, and each one inhabits a lonely world. The ambient atmosphere pulls the piano into an orbit where it’s free to turn and swirl; a radiant ballet, and without the restrictive law of gravity to shackle it. The surrounding atmosphere, brought about by a vacuum of synth and a set of chiming electronics which flirt with new age music, is a dark expanse over which the piano may play. Space is the ultimate playground, and in the piano, Chan adds a twinkle of colour, creating splashes of light which predate time, returning to the dawn of starlight and the Big Bang itself. At other times, such as ‘Sturmfrei’, a celestial ambient comes to take over, gleaming with a sci-fi sheen, like something from Halo. ‘Hiraeth’ is equally stunning, and the closing strings provide a comforting end. Exceptionally warm and delivered from the heart despite a pursuit of the monolithic, Chan’s music lights up the world and beyond. What is life without emotion, and living without loving? Chan’s music is emotional and mega in scale, but there’s a beautiful intimacy, too. The Universe may be vast beyond all measure, but the heart’s capacity for love is infinite, no matter how small its cage, aka, the body. Everything has a place, regardless of size. Inklings turn into dreams. Thousand-mile journeys begin with a single step. A butterfly spreads her wings in Asia and a hurricane sweeps through Florida. Everything and everyone starts somewhere, and there’s infinite value in that. There’s also something comforting in being so little; Earth’s children wrapped up in the spiral arms of the Milky Way, a mother to a child. www.norvik.bandcamp.com

items.body: Canadian electronic and experimental composer Tim Hecker is dropping his ninth solo album, Konoyo, on September 28 through Kranky, and it comes after the label’s reissuing and remastering of his earlier Haunt Me, Haunt Me, Do It Again and Radio Amor. Konoyo’s soul is rooted in Japan, where, in a temple on the outskirts of Tokyo, Hecker collaborated with members from the Gagaku Ensemble Tokyo Gakuso, gagaku being an ancient form of Japanese classical music – ‘elegant music’ – performed for many centuries at the Imperial Court. As a result, Konoyo offers an immediate change of mood. Konoyo is a response. Concerned with negative space and a continued concern for music’s ‘increasingly banal density’, Konoyo’s timbre is one of constriction, its mood sombre, akin to a lost kingdom and a crown that’s faded from its once-burnt gold. Strings are stretched to breaking point, but they’re still able to shine with a dull radiance, are still beautiful in their crystalline gleaming and their cavernous echoes, managing to sound strangely harmonious even in ongoing anguish. The sound is refined in its elegant, controlled falls, its growling low tones and rivers of grit; its squeals of unease and dissatisfaction are similar in tone to the inky darkness of Ravedeath, 1972. Tracks pick up extra tonal layers along the way, and they suddenly populate the music, clanking thickly with the heavy air of ceremony. On ‘Keyed Out’, the track mutates halfway in, starting off in menacing territory, segueing into a quiet stretch where nothing moves, before adding in an array of electronic sounds. The album addresses decay – which, in the physical world, is inevitable – but it’s more to do with the decay of a crushed spirit, examining a growing dissatisfaction with music in its current state and the falling away of all things. In Konoyo, something is failing, something is struggling; burning out. And because of that, it feels radically different, at times tired and at other times angry, and thus alive. As they slow down, the notes lose some of their vitality, energy draining like a spent battery, becoming dense glitch-hieroglyphics and mirage-like squares; you have to squint in order to see them. But the sounds are still able to gleam, shining like the sharp blade of a katana in the dark, a brandished sliver of light in a black cage. The tones seem to be running wild – multiple sources overlap, crushing others, but they never feel like they’re in competition with one another – and Hecker tempers the numerous sounds to great effect, retaining a crestfallen mood inside its tight locket despite the occasional rush-hours within the record. In September, the regal sense of decay is given extra emphasis. Autumn, when nature relinquishes, sleeps, and dies with a bang, a flourishing display of might and majesty. Similar things happen in the darkened labyrinth of Konoyo’s temple, its reverent music dominated by a pervasive feeling of tilted discord and ambient loss. Dissolving like sodium, like acid rain pounding the street, the music glows like a halogen, offering a wink of light and nothing more; refusing to offer more. The thumping, slow-bleeding percussion on closing track ‘Across to Anoyo’ is strong at first, but even this succumbs and dissolves, eroding like a corpse in its coffin. The ennui is pervasive. Despite its restrictions, Konoyo is more than generous. Its long running time and its spectacular tonal array is something of a wonder, untameable as always, even if its mood is adamantly downcast. Hecker will stage a series of special performances in tandem with the album’s release, featuring members of the Gagaku ensemble on sh?, ryuteki and hichiriki, accompanied by Kara-Lis Coverdale. Live dates: Oct 2 – Tokyo WWWX Oct 6 – London Barbican Oct 7 – Krakow Unsound Oct 8 – Berlin Funkhaus www.kranky.net www.timhecker.bandcamp.com

items.body: (You are here) Somewhere With his latest work, (You are here) Somewhere, part of a new flurry of releases on Impulsive Habitat, Bruno Duplant seems to have given us an aural adaptation of Marc Augé’s famous book Non-Places: Introduction to an Anthropology of Supermodernity (1995)… In his essay, Augé theorized the idea of the “non-place, the ambivalent space that has none of the familiar attributes of place and which incites no sense of belonging.” What he investigated, were not only those generic spaces necessary to the accelerated circulation of goods and people, such as airports and bus terminals, but also those anonymous “rest and recreation” environments such as chain hotels and shopping malls, which can be found anywhere in the globalised world. This idea is certainly not new and has been looked at before. I am thinking of Simon Whetham’s Mall Muzac (Unfathomless, 2011), for instance, where Whetham captured recordings in The Mall, Broadmead, Bristol. And yet, Duplant’s album is still an effective exercise in sonic dislocation, a timely reminder of the increasingly depersonalized landscape, the ever increasing gentrification of many urban centers the world over, is bringing about. The French composer and sound artist makes no concessions, collecting “sounds from everywhere. From inside & outside” and offers them raw, with no treatment. The result is both familiar and destabilizing. I found myself trying to latch on to any recognizable sounds, such as snippets of conversation in languages that seemed identifiable, in order to give some concrete domesticity to this alienating “Somewhere”. Ultimately, the sonic environment captured by Dupont is the aural equivalent of stock images from picture libraries, too mundane and immediately accessible to have any real meaning. It is only valid as a sort of shortcut to suggest transit and idleness. Snatches of Excerpts of baroque music, for instance, were never going to act as a geographical compass. There is no definite indication of any timeframe either. The sound of what could be crickets introduces a seasonal marker, but the uncertainty of whether this might belong to an interior space quickly transforms it into a mechanical buzz. Birdsongs merges with a busy fuzziness punctuated by beeps that subverts any pastoral suggestion. And yet, I found myself back in the countryside with more cricket song. An unedited recurring mobile phone interference suggests that the kind of aural anthropology of daily life pursued by Duplant cannot be approached without taking into account the pervasive connectivity we are trapped in. The irony being that there is nothing here I could connect with. Or rather, I could connect with so much, as to make the whole exercise meaningless. By the time I could distinctly detect a few words of French spoken towards the end of the second part, I was beyond caring, even though, finding out where I was supposed to be, should never have been the goal of this listening experience. This “Somewhere” is not somewhere I long to spend time in. But sometimes it is important to be reminded of this. (You are here) Somewhere by Bruno Duplant is available as a free download on Impulsive Habitat. www.impulsivehabitat.com

After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
